title: Modeling Perceived Promptness in Simultaneous Interpreting from Quality, Structure, and Timing Signals
author: Ziyu Zhang, Satoshi Nakamura
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28566v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simultaneous interpreting requires interpreters to convey the source accurately while keeping pace with it in real time. Timing measures such as segment-onset delay capture part of this requirement, but may not fully reflect how professional evaluators judge promptness. We investigate whether these judgments can be explained by timing alone or whether the interpreted output provides additional information. Our dataset contains 622 Chinese-English and English-Chinese segments from 16 source speeches and seven interpreters. Two senior professional interpreters rated each segment for language quality (LQ), expressiveness (EXP), and perceived latency (LAT), which we also refer to as professional promptness. On held-out source speeches, onset delay alone achieves a Pearson correlation of r = .318 with LAT ratings. Combining predicted LQ and EXP with delay improves the correlation to r = .475. Lexical and structural features provide a stronger signal, reaching r = .632 when combined with delay and r = .658 when predicted quality is also included. These results suggest that professional promptness judgments reflect properties of the interpreted output beyond when the interpreter begins speaking. The additional contribution of predicted quality over structural features, however, is modest. Although the two evaluators differ in how strongly quality relates to LAT, cross-evaluator predictions remain positively correlated with LAT ratings. The overall pattern also holds when each interpreter is held out in turn.

takeaways: Combining predicted LQ and EXP with delay improves the correlation to r = .475.
Lexical and structural features provide a stronger signal, reaching r = .632 when combined with delay and r = .658 when predicted quality is also included.
These results suggest that professional promptness judgments reflect properties of the interpreted output beyond when the interpreter begins speaking.
The additional contribution of predicted quality over structural features, however, is modest.

title: MedCoast: Semantic Abstraction of Reasoning Trajectories for Test-Time Biomedical Question Answering
author: Yishan Zhong, Jieru Li, Xuanzhe Ding, Shaunna Wang, Yanxin Yang, Micky C. Nnamdi, J. Ben Tamo, Yifei Wang, Yining Yuan, Benoit L. Marteau, Shaun Q. Y. Tan, Carrie Moore, Luyu Xie, Yang Xie, Wenqi Shi, May D. Wang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28586v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Biomedical question answering often requires multi-step reasoning under limited inference budgets. While test-time search methods such as Tree-of-Thought can improve reasoning performance, directly searching over free-form language is computationally expensive and highly redundant, as many reasoning trajectories contain semantically equivalent intermediate steps expressed in different surface forms. We introduce MedCoast, an offline-to-online reasoning framework that converts sampled chain-of-thought trajectories into a compact space for structured process supervision. Offline, we recursively cluster semantically similar reasoning steps under shared prefixes to construct an abstract reasoning tree that captures recurring clinical reasoning patterns. We then derive node-level supervision from progress toward correct solutions, and train a lightweight process reward model (PRM) to evaluate partial reasoning states. At inference time, the learned critic guides test-time exploration by prioritizing promising reasoning prefixes. Across seven biomedical QA benchmarks, MedCoast often improves over self-consistency under fixed inference budgets, with gains of up to 15 points. Despite using a reward model more than 50 times smaller, MedCoast achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art reward models in several settings, highlighting its potential for resource-constrained biomedical reasoning.

title: Reducing Permutation Sensitivity in Multimodal Large Language Models via Shared Positions and Attention-Only Distillation
author: Yifei Cheng, Xiaolin Zhang, Yu-Xuan Qiu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28612v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we conduct a systematic study on improving permutation robustness while preserving accuracy. First, we categorize permutation bias phenomena into four representative scenarios. Then, we take the multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) dataset as an example under text-option reordering scenario to analyze the root cause of permutation bias. Based on this root cause analysis and set encoding strategy, we investigate shared positions with blocked cross-unit attention (SP-B) and extend this design to bidirectional cross-unit attention (SP-V) for modality exchange. However, these structural changes may reduce predictive accuracy. To recover model capability across different scenarios under the SP structure, an attention-only distillation from frozen native models is proposed. Shared positions reduce permutation sensitivity, and attention-only distillation improves accuracy under the shared-position structure. Across all three models, our method is comparable to or better than majority voting in macro-average all-permutation accuracy, and outperforms supervised fine-tuning by 1.95-4.20 percentage points. This work provides valuable insight into permutation bias mitigation and model capability recovery.

title: WISP: Composable Representations for Wrist-Worn Activity Recognition
author: Zipeng Wu, Shiqiao Zhou, Fabian Spill, James Andrews
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28033v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Smartwatches and fitness bands are among the most common wearable devices, and large national health studies record movement at the wrist. Yet existing human activity recognition benchmarks mix sensors worn on different parts of the body, so they do not show how well activities can be recognised from the wrist alone. We introduce WristHARBench, a benchmark that standardises participant-disjoint evaluation across nine wrist-acceleration datasets and two additional multichannel inertial datasets. We hypothesise that different human activities leave complementary patterns in wrist motion, such as local shape, rhythm, temporal order and cross-axis relationships, and propose WISP (Wrist-Informed Space of Predictive Representations), a composable representation space that combines representations of these patterns with compatible classifiers. Across the nine primary datasets, WISP with random search achieves 70.20% mean Macro-F1, compared with 59.62% for the strongest of 18 external baselines. Controlled ablations and baseline comparisons indicate that recognition improves mainly when a representation adds motion patterns that the others lack, rather than when it represents the same pattern in a different way.

title: Measuring and Teaching Language Model Agents to Act on Delayed Consequences
author: Shardul Bansal, Seth Schilbe, Jarrod Barnes
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28158v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language model agents are increasingly asked to run ongoing multi-day operations rather than finish isolated single-turn tasks. In daily operations, today's choices reshape later observations and cash constraints because empty shelves hide lost walk-in demand, short-shipped customers quietly shrink future orders weeks later, and emergency buying drains working capital. We introduce SMB Bench, a calibrated 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and an 859-run frontier trace dataset, to ask what experience and learning signal make an agent better at noticing, attributing, and acting on the delayed consequences of its own decisions in unseen businesses. Across 16 frontier models, only 3 outperform a fixed buying rule; models often record a relevant diagnosis in their notes without changing later purchases in time, showing that diagnosing a problem, changing behavior, and improving a business are separate achievements. To study how experience improves those failures in an open model (Qwen3.8-27B), we used training-business records to identify operational rules and archived frontier quarters as starting states to continue from rather than transcripts to copy. On an unseen test business under identical evaluation instructions, the trained policy followed customer-protection commitments more consistently and reduced severe-loss quarters, while the additional profit benefit remained uncertain. Carrying those commitments through the quarter exposed the cost of fulfilling them, as early-quarter stocking habits left the buyer relying on emergency supply and a deteriorating supplier. The results separate recognizing a delayed effect, acting on it consistently, and coordinating surrounding decisions so that the response improves profit. SMB Bench connects these observations to a learning method by turning archived decisions and their consequences into reusable training experience.

title: RefineKV: Query-Adaptive KV Cache Compression via Attention-Error Bounds
author: Kewei Lian, Jiayi Zhai, Anji Liu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28171v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Repeatedly accessing the full key--value (KV) cache is a major bottleneck in long-context language model decoding. We find that small query-specific subsets can accurately approximate full attention, yet their union covers nearly the entire cache, motivating query-adaptive access for the KV cache. A natural approach is to split the KV cache into clusters, using compact representatives for clusters that incur negligible error while expanding the rest to their original KV entries. We derive a selection criterion from an upper bound on attention-output error, which reveals two complementary factors governing the error: importance measures the impact of a cluster, while distortion measures how faithfully the cluster can be represented. Based on this criterion, we propose RefineKV, a decoding-time query-adaptive KV compression method. Experiments on two models and three benchmarks demonstrate that RefineKV retains near-full-attention quality while achieving up to 7.6x speedup in the attention phase and 1.66x faster decoding, establishing a new quality-latency Pareto frontier.

title: A world model for longitudinal health-trajectory prediction in older adults across multinational cohorts
author: Jingyi Wu, Chenghua Guo, Qianlin Zuo, Pengfei Li, Luxia Zhang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aging is characterized by continuously evolving health states, yet most existing prediction models focus on static health risk at isolated time points rather than explicitly modelling how health trajectories unfold over time. We developed a health world model based on the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture to represent evolving health states and simulate future trajectories under specified actions. The model combines a state encoder, an action- and context-conditioned predictor, a stop-gradient target encoder, and clinical outcome heads. We trained the model on the US Health and Retirement Study (HRS) and evaluated it without refitting in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS). Open-loop evaluation assessed discrimination and calibration for mortality and worsening of activities of daily living (ADL) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL). In the held-out HRS test set, the areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) for mortality, ADL worsening, and IADL worsening were 0.89, 0.93, and 0.93 at the first horizon and 0.84, 0.84, and 0.85 at the fifth horizon, respectively. Predicted risks stratified subsequent outcomes across horizons. Across the evaluated horizons, mortality AUROC ranged from 0.867 to 0.881 in ELSA and from 0.796 to 0.801 in CHARLS. Simulated trajectories preserved the expected risk ordering across predefined action regimes. In counterfactual simulations, changes in lifestyle actions shifted predicted risks in directions consistent with observed associations. The model provides a framework for longitudinal risk prediction and action-conditioned simulation in older adults.

title: Feedback Shortcut: Speculative Decoding for Latent Feedback Transformers
author: Benhao Huang, Xuezhe Ma, Hector Liu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28227v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Feeding each position's top-layer hidden state back into the next position's input improves Transformer performance. However, this feedback breaks speculative decoding, since verifying a drafted token requires the top-layer state from its preceding position, which forces the draft to rely on an approximate stand-in. Training the model to adapt to this stand-in can lower the exact-decoding performance ceiling, while using it at inference time further introduces approximation error. We propose Feedback Shortcut to address both bottlenecks. First, state alignment trains a lightweight projection from multi-token prediction head states to stand-ins, leaving base model training untouched. Second, pipelined correction re-evaluates each draft using its predecessor's newly computed state, a much closer proxy to true feedback. Running this correction inside the verification pass of subsequent drafts improves accuracy with zero extra calls. Across 135M and 780M scales, Feedback Shortcut stays within $10^{-4}$ bits per byte of the exact-decoding ceiling on Paloma and accelerates decoding by 2.4-2.8x with about 2% more training compute than the latent feedback Transformer. At large batch sizes, skipping correction still preserves Transformer speed and over 80% of latent feedback's gains.

title: Learning the Projection onto the Data Support: Distribution Learning that Avoids Memorization
author: Lin Chen, Dejan Slep\v{c}ev
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a framework for learning distributions supported on manifolds based on estimating the nearest-point projection onto the data support. Specifically, we define an objective functional over a class of functions whose minimizer recovers this projection. The proposed framework automatically adapts to the intrinsic dimension and allows for data supported on unions of manifolds with varying dimensions. The resulting objective can be optimized using standard neural network architectures. We present population-level results establishing recovery of the manifold projection and prove finite-sample Wasserstein generalization bounds. Furthermore, we validate the approach empirically across a range of settings. In contrast to widely used generative models such as diffusion models, whose objectives can be minimized by memorizing training samples, our formulation excludes such behavior. We also introduce a direct memorization metric to verify that the learned projection generates new samples rather than reproducing the training set.

title: The Cross-Context Threshold Test: Detecting Discrimination Under Environmental Shifts
author: Jun Yuan, Xinyue Ye
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28259v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how threshold tests for detecting discrimination under environmental shifts, focusing on the Veil-of-Darkness (VoD) setting where visibility changes between daylight and darkness. We show that standard threshold tests, when applied separately to daylight and darkness data, violate key assumptions: risk distributions drift across contexts and thresholds fluctuate arbitrarily. We propose a cross-context threshold test that enforces distributional invariance and monotonic threshold decay. Using New York City stop-and-frisk data and synthetic experiments, we demonstrate that this model yields more reliable thresholds, improves bias detection, and aligns with the counterfactual logic of the VoD test. Our framework generalizes to fairness auditing whenever environmental context influences decisions.

title: FoGConcept: Identifying Interpretable Movement Concepts for Freezing-of-Gait Detection from Multi-Scale IMU Signals
author: Chuntian Chi, John Clapham, GinaMari Blackwell, Leslie Cloud, Ingrid Pretzer-Aboff, Yanfu Zhang, Huajie Shao, Gang Zhou
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28262v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Freezing of gait (FoG) is a disabling motor symptom of Parkinson's disease, characterized by an episodic inability to initiate or sustain effective stepping. Current inertial measurement unit (IMU)-based models can detect FoG accurately, but they fail to explain their predictions in terms of human-understandable movement concepts. A major contribution of this work is to identify nine human-understandable movement concepts encoded by a multi-scale FoG model, including gait initiation, rhythmic bilateral gait, trembling in place, shuffling steps, and pivot turns. These concepts recur across subjects, are functionally linked to the model's FoG decisions, and exhibit emergent specialization across short and long temporal contexts. Repeating the concept-discovery procedure on a new FoG dataset, wider temporal contexts, and a deeper backbone recovers the same comparatively stable set of movement concepts. Accordingly, we propose FoGConcept, a mechanism-based interpretability framework for learning movement concepts from multi-scale IMU signals. Domain experts independently recognize 88.9% of the identified concepts, while the proposed model achieves an F1 score of 94.2% for FoG detection. Our findings show that accurate FoG detection can be understood through human-recognizable movement patterns, providing new insight into what a detection model learns to distinguish FoG from non-FoG movement.

title: Failure Modes and Data-Efficient Remedies for Transformer-Based Prediction of Viscoplastic Flows
author: Maedeh Saberi, Hugo Franca, Maziyar Jalaal, Safa Jamali
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28267v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fast and accurate prediction of viscoplastic flows remains a challenge in computational rheology due to yield surfaces, discontinuous gradients, and strongly nonlinear transitions between yielded and unyielded regions. Transformer-based neural operators such as RheOFormer have recently shown strong potential for surrogate modeling of non-Newtonian flows. However, their applicability to viscoplastic systems and their efficacy in recovering realistic flows remain poorly understood. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of RheOFormer applied to steady Bingham channel flow. By isolating the problem to a simple geometry and constitutive model, we examine how dataset structure, numerical value range, and input representation govern the model's ability to interpolate and extrapolate within the parameter space. The data regimes in which RheOFormer remains accurate and those in which errors emerge are identified, particularly for plug-dominated flows and for conditions outside the velocity scales or flow structures represented during training. Upon identifying these failure modes, targeted enhancements to the input representation and loss formulation are introduced to better predict low-gradient plug regions. Logarithmic velocity representations and gradient-aware loss formulations substantially improve accuracy in challenging regimes where the baseline formulation fails. In addition, extrapolation errors are reduced by augmenting the training set with only a few strategically selected cases spanning the missing physical regimes. Finally, a single partially developed snapshot suffices for an accurate steady-state prediction, and the model outperforms simply copying its input throughout flow development. These results highlight the importance of appropriate field representation and parameter-space coverage for data-efficient neural-operator prediction of viscoplastic flows.

title: SONATI: Spatio-temporal ocean neighbourhood asymmetric transformer for imputation of sparse, tabular data with uncertainty
author: Yvonne Jenniges, Boris Peter Koch, Maike Sonnewald, Sebastian Maneth
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Missing value imputation is often a prerequisite for downstream analyses. In oceanography, observational data are frequently structured in a tabular manner, highly sparse and exhibit spatio-temporal structures that classical imputers such as k-nearest neighbours or MissForest are not suited to exploit. We present the Spatio-temporal Ocean Neighbourhood Asymmetric Transformer for Imputation (SONATI), a masked, factorised time-space transformer operating on pre-computed, local time and space neighbourhoods, which reduces computational complexity compared to global attention. SONATI is designed to work with tabular data and is thus in principle able to work on both gridded and unstructured data, though evaluation here was performed on gridded North Atlantic data only. It provides aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties through a negative log-likelihood loss and multiple forward passes with Monte Carlo dropout. Systematic ablations on attention type and masking strategies guided the final architecture design. The results showed that SONATI outperformed classical and transformer-based methods by at least 12.5% in terms of root mean squared error (RMSE) on a large observational oceanographic dataset with key biogeochemical and physical parameters in the North Atlantic (potential temperature, salinity, oxygen, nitrate, silicate and phosphate). Attention type and masking strategy strongly affected imputation accuracy and smoothness of the produced oceanographic fields. Best results were achieved by factorised time-space attention and combined geographic and per-sample masking. The combined masking strategy reduced the imputation error by 14.3% compared to per-sample masking only. Uncertainties were moderately well calibrated (miscalibration area at observed locations $0.074\pm0.012$) and moderately correlated with the imputation error.

title: What Do Differentiable Rule Learners Need? FLARE: Fuzzy Rules with Additive Evidence
author: Javier Fumanal-Idocin, Javier Andreu-Perez
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28272v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rule learners are used where transparency and accountability are required, because they give practitioners patterns they can read. Learning rules is a discrete problem, so neurosymbolic pipelines that use rules as explanations rely on relaxations such as the straight-through estimator. However, these differentiable rule learners often lag behind both classical rule learners and black-box classifiers in terms of performance. We study which parts of a rule-based classifier affect performance, and how well gradient-based training learns each of them. We found that most of the performance comes from how the rules are weighted: random rules with learned weights are already more accurate than every published differentiable rule learner we tested. Based on our results, we propose FLARE (Fuzzy Learned-Antecedent Rule Evidence), a differentiable rule learner that learns simple rules that combine to make the final decision. title: Scalable Beckmann Maps Improve One-step Generation
author: Ulrik Unneberg, Shiyi Wang, Lee Cheuk-Kit, Felix Berg, Boris Kozinsky, Yilun Du, Michael S. Albergo, Eric Vanden-Eijnden
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Beckmann Transport Models (BTM) learn one-step generative maps end-to-end from data, without a teacher, a distillation stage, or pretrained features. We introduce Scalable Beckmann Maps (SBM), which bring to BTM the two ingredients behind the quality of modern multistep generators: classifier-free guidance (CFG) and a training recipe that scales, while keeping sampling at a single network evaluation. CFG combines conditional and unconditional velocity or score predictions, which a Beckmann map does not have. Our guidance rests on one observation: the BTM current is a positive multiple of an autonomous denoising field, to which CFG applies as it does to a velocity. With exact denoisers this gives guided BTM. In practice we substitute the map's own conditional and null predictions for the denoisers, which requires no additional network and introduces a bias that we characterize. We show that the guided update is consistent with a guided conservation equation, and that guidance can move the boundaries between basins, sending more noise to the modes a condition favors. Trained from scratch in the latent of a representation autoencoder, SBM reaches a one-step FID of 1.6 on ImageNet 256x256 without a teacher or a feature loss, outperforming the Improved-MeanFlow baseline with 3.2x fewer FLOPs. In text-to-image generation it reaches a GenEval score of 0.86 with one network evaluation. As a world model, where we train without guidance, the recipe alone outperforms DriftWorld on all five metrics of two robot-manipulation benchmarks, with 1.9-2.8x less training compute and no pretrained auxiliary feature encoder.

title: Benchmarking EEG feature families for ADHD research in children and adolescents: performance and explainability across attention tasks
author: Javier Sanchis, Jorge Garc\'ia-Carrasco, \'Alvaro Navarro, Tahar Kechadi, Juan Trujillo
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder varies in presentation. Diagnosis requires clinical and developmental assessment. Reproducible electroencephalography measures may complement clinical and behavioural characterisation, but differing feature definitions and evaluation methods hinder comparison. We compared seven feature families and four combinations across attention tasks and assessed the stability of held-out explanations. Two serious games yielded four overlapping attention-task cohorts of 123-140 participants each. Repeated nested participant-held-out evaluation assessed recruitment-group discrimination. Exploratory paired participant-cluster bootstrap tests corrected for multiplicity in two separate families: 72 individual-task contrasts and 18 fusion contrasts. For eight configurations selected after inspecting predictive results, we explained held-out native probabilities before calibration. In the strongest task context, the highest configuration mean AUROC over three repetitions was 0.773, with a fixed-prediction 95% interval of 0.692-0.854 unadjusted for selecting the maximum. Precision, sensitivity and specificity were 0.740, 0.556 and 0.861. In that task, the paired AUROC difference for connectivity minus spectral features averaged +0.2083 across six classifiers and the common 8 s and 16 s durations, with pointwise 95% CI 0.1076-0.3072 and adjusted p = 0.0036. F4-AF4 beta-band coherence led repetition-level attribution summaries in five selected procedures and was selected in every fit. Other contexts showed weaker discrimination and less consistent retention of leading scientific inputs. No general classifier winner emerged. Connectivity and its recurring coherence input warrant independent replication, but do not justify a universal feature recommendation. These exploratory findings do not establish causal task effects, disease mechanisms or diagnostic validity.

title: AV-FLARE: Feature-Level Reliability Estimation for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
author: Ines Jemmali, Alaa Nfissi, Wassim Bouachir, Nizar Bouguila
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28327v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition (MMER) systems typically rely on learned feature representations and attention mechanisms that implicitly weight information across time and modalities. However, these mechanisms do not explicitly incorporate input reliability, despite the presence of noise in audio, occlusions in visual data, and the sparse and event-driven nature of affective cues. We propose AV-FLARE, a framework that explicitly estimates fine-grained reliability scores across both temporal and feature dimensions prior to temporal modeling and uses them to modulate feature representations. Reliability is computed using two complementary components: (i) a supervised network trained jointly with the classification objective, and (ii) an unsupervised Gaussian Mixture Model that models global feature distributions. These signals are combined to provide both task-driven and distribution-aware reliability estimates. To integrate modalities, we introduce a hierarchical cross-modal attention mechanism in which textual features are used to guide audio-visual fusion as a semantic reference modality. Experiments on the IEMOCAP dataset show that AV-FLARE improves over a no-reliability baseline, achieving 90.81\% accuracy and 81.69\% F1-score, corresponding to gains of +4.41% and +8.56%, respectively. These results suggest that incorporating explicit input reliability estimation may improve robustness in multimodal emotion recognition under the evaluated setting.

title: TabK: Amortized Bayesian Estimation of the Number of Clusters in Tabular Data
author: Mohammadreza Bakhtyari, Bogdan Mazoure, Renato Cordeiro de Amorim, Guillaume Rabusseau, Vladimir Makarenkov
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28335v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Estimating the number of clusters, $k$, is a fundamental prerequisite for most clustering algorithms. Traditionally, this estimation has relied on computationally expensive grid searches over internal cluster validity indices (CVIs) or adaptive clustering algorithms, both constrained by specific statistical assumptions. We introduce TabK, a zero-shot, permutation-invariant transformer architecture that frames the estimation of $k$ as an amortized Bayesian inference problem for tabular data. TabK leverages a novel Quantile Feature Encoder (QFE) to extract position-free, content-derived representations from empirical marginal distributions. By learning a generalized structural bias over a diverse synthetic prior, TabK estimates the number of clusters in a single forward pass per ensemble member. Evaluated across 50 diverse real-world benchmarks, TabK outperforms all competing methods, achieving a mean absolute error (MAE) value of 1.04 compared to 2.14 for the closest competitor. TabK also achieves the lowest average inference time, producing estimates in less than one second on average and running $2\times$ faster than TabClustPFN and $30\times$ faster than traditional CVIs such as Silhouette and Calinski-Harabasz. Code is available at https://github.com/mrbakhtyari/TabK.

title: Which Loans, Not How Many: Exactly Level-Invariant, Anytime-Valid Monitoring of Deployed Risk Models
author: Xin Xu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A refinancing wave can change the number of mortgage prepayments without changing the relationship between scores and prepayment. In a logistic model, conditioning on the monthly count removes the intercept from the likelihood of which loans prepay. Our fixed-start slope product tests a lower bound on the calibration slope. At threshold 20 its probability of ever crossing under the null is at most 5%. The restarted level sum tracks departures from intercept tolerance. A confidence sequence estimates a constant slope, and the restart-intersection rule detects changes in that slope. A continuous mixture avoids the off-grid width floor of a discrete prior. On Freddie Mac loans, fixed-slope resampling reproduces 78% of maintained-model monthly AUC variance in development and 70% in the holdout (95% intervals 57-100% and 48-100%). From fresh holdout starts, the restarted level sum crosses on both paths, and the fixed-start slope product stays below threshold on both. The restart-intersection rule signals a downward change for the frozen model in April 2018 and an upward change for the maintained model in a supplementary run in August 2019.

title: Toward Adversarially Robust World Models
author: Ethan Rathbun, Jonathan N\"other, Christopher Amato, Alina Oprea, Goran Radanovi\'c
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28345v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Latent dynamic world models have proven to be highly versatile tools for embodied artificial intelligence systems, enabling online action planning, safe policy evaluation, and scalable policy learning. However, this versatility makes world models a vulnerable and centralized point of failure as a compromised model can impact planning, evaluation, and training at once. Therefore it is critical that the security and robustness properties of world models are properly understood before they are universally deployed in embodied AI systems. In this work we take a unifying approach towards this understanding, developing two novel attacks against world models, named state hallucination and dynamic shift attacks, aimed directly at impacting downstream systems, and proposing a new theoretical lens through which to study the robustness of latent dynamic world models. Through our analysis we identify robust latent space encoders as the key component of robust world models. We empirically validate this finding on four separate latent dynamic world model families, studying Dino World Model, Le World Model, r2Dreamer, and Cosmos 3, demonstrating significant improvements in robustness through adversarial encoder model training.

title: Coupling-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Co-Evolving Graph Games
author: Mina Kim, Guanghui Lan, Benoit Montreuil
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building hydrogen station networks, electric vehicle charging grids, or vaccine distribution systems requires coordinating two separately operated graphs, demand-side facilities and the supply-side networks they depend on, where each operator's payoff depends on the other's choices. We formalize this as the Co-Evolving Graph Game (CEGG), a setting that sits between facility location, interdependent-network analysis, and graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) but is not jointly addressed by any of them. We propose Cross-Graph Attention with Policy Mirror Descent (CGA-PMD), pairing cross-graph attention, which lets each agent read only the partner-graph nodes structurally coupled to its own, with a policy mirror descent update for stable training. Across three reward domains and a range of practical network scales, we find that the structure of the coupling selects which method wins: at small scale most methods are competitive, but as scale grows or coupling becomes irregular, CGA-PMD is the one method that stays reliable: it attains the highest success count on each of five real city networks, while own-only, unmasked-attention, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based variants degrade in distinct ways. Our theoretical analysis addresses the optimizer side: the Kullback-Leibler (KL)-regularized update admits an iteration-uniform cumulative drift bound, whereas the clip update admits no such bound on the iterations where the clip does not bind. The implementation is available at https://github.com/Mina-Kim-Github/cegg-cga-pmd.

title: Cross-Site Transformers Are Robust Heart Rate Estimators
author: Mason Kadem, Rong Zheng
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28366v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Single-site heart-rate estimation from photoplethysmography (PPG) degrades sharply under real-world motion. Multi-site PPG provides a natural solution, but existing models fuse sites as generic sensor channels rather than exploiting their hemodynamic structure: each heartbeat propagates along the arterial tree, appearing across body sites as delayed and transformed copies of the same cardiac event. We propose the Cross-Site Transformer, which introduces a hemodynamically informed inductive bias by restricting multi-sensor fusion to cross-attention between PPG sites. On WildPPG, the largest in-the-wild benchmark available, our model establishes a new single-model state of the art, reducing error by 21% over the previous best and 35% over the best prior transformer. The same cross-site restriction makes the trained network directly auditable. Because each cross-attention head lies on one directed pathway between sites, causal resample ablation can isolate and test each direction of information flow. Ablating the chest-to-wrist pathway doubles error, whereas the reverse costs far less. Encoding hemodynamic structure into attention routing thus improves real-world sensing robustness and enables rigorous auditing of multi-sensor fusion.

title: Data-Dependent Probability Estimation via Sample Amplification
author: Vitaly Feldman, Satyen Kale, Mahbod Majid, Kunal Talwar
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.28399v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can we estimate the probability of an event chosen after seeing the data, without using any fresh samples? Its empirical probability can be arbitrarily misleading, while learning the entire distribution to constant accuracy requires $\Theta(d)$ samples on a domain of size $d$. We show that $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d})$ samples suffice for constant mean squared error, provided the rule choosing the event is known. More generally, our estimator handles arbitrary $[0,1]$-valued queries and runs in polynomial time given evaluation access to the rule. This sample complexity matches the known lower bound up to logarithmic factors and resolves the open question posed by Feldman, Kale, Raman, Talwar, and Tewari (arXiv:2610.41244). Our estimation framework relies on a new combination of sample amplification (arXiv:1904.12053 and arXiv:2201.04315) with distribution learning via online optimization. Our estimator achieves mean squared error $O(d^{3/4}/n)$ when $d\leq n$ and $\widetilde{O}(d^{1/4}/\sqrt{n})$ when $d>n$. We complement this with a lower bound of $\Omega(\min\{1,\sqrt{d}/n\})$ on the mean squared error. Using our framework, we also design an efficient estimator for data-dependent queries on Gaussian distributions with unknown mean and identity covariance. Finally, we show that a smoothed variant of the problem is much (exponentially) easier. For discrete distributions, if the sample size is chosen uniformly from $\{n,\ldots,2n-1\}$, then $n=O(\log d)$ suffices for constant mean squared error.

title: Agentic Discovery of Soundness Bugs in Safe Rust Bindings
author: Marius Momeu
contentSnippet: Rust crates confine unsafe code, such as calls into C or C++ libraries or system calls, behind safe interfaces that must uphold Rust's invariants. If an interface encodes one rule of the code beneath it too weakly, a program written in purely safe Rust can cause undefined behavior. Static analyzers and fuzzers are bound to fixed patterns or to the paths they execute. We propose LLM agents as auditors of these interfaces, and study how well they do it. We first define a taxonomy of the defects of such interfaces, including undefined behavior, divergences from the wrapped library, and incomplete unsafe contracts. We then measure, in repeated audits of a real-world crate by a closed and an open model, Claude Opus 5.5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which defect classes agents find, how well they triage them, and what makes them find more. Agents find the first two classes unprompted, but find few incomplete contracts even when asked. Their findings are almost always real, even without an independent reviewer, yet they lack triage discipline: they seldom confirm with a sanitizer, and they stop early. With the same guidance, the open model finds as many defects as the closed one at a quarter of the cost. We integrate these insights in Crustify, an agentic system for automating C-to-Rust tasks, and run it at scale. In 16 widely used crates, including the bindings to the C libraries OpenSSL, SQLite, libgit2, and libcurl and to the C++ engine V8, Crustify found 225 undefined-behavior bugs, 23 behavioral divergences, and 36 incomplete unsafe contracts, between 3 and 61 per crate at a median cost under $50 per audit. In the Linux kernel's Rust abstractions, it found 11 more undefined-behavior bugs and 4 incomplete contracts. Maintainers have fixed 26 of the 83 findings that we reported.

We propose LLM agents as auditors of these interfaces, and study how well they do it. We first define a taxonomy of the defects of such interfaces, including undefined behavior, divergences from the wrapped library, and incomplete unsafe contracts. We then measure, in repeated audits of a real-world crate by a closed and an open model, Claude Opus 5.5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which defect classes agents find, how well they triage them, and what makes them find more.
takeaways: Agents find the first two classes unprompted, but find few incomplete contracts even when asked.
Their findings are almost always real, even without an independent reviewer, yet they lack triage discipline: they seldom confirm with a sanitizer, and they stop early.
With the same guidance, the open model finds as many defects as the closed one at a quarter of the cost.
We integrate these insights in Crustify, an agentic system for automating C-to-Rust tasks, and run it at scale.

title: Amazon acquires key assets of AI startup Decart for reported $7.5B
author: Maria Deutscher
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 20:40 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026

Amazon acquires key assets of AI startup Decart for reported $7.5B

Amazon.com Inc. today announced plans to hire the technical staff of startup Decart.AI Inc. and acquire its core technology.

The company didn’t disclose the terms of the deal. However, sources told Bloomberg that Amazon is paying about $7.5 billion. That’s nearly twice the valuation Decart reportedly received after its most recent funding round in May.

In August, reports emerged that the company had drawn takeover interest from Anthropic PBC. The artificial intelligence provider reportedly sought to buy Decart for $6 billion but walked away from the deal in September. Rumors that Amazon could swoop in emerged the following month.

Decart founders Dean Leitersdorf, Moshe Shalev and Orian Leitersdorf will join the tech giant along with Decart’s research team. Additionally, Amazon is acquiring the technology behind the company’s DOS platform, which helps boost the efficiency of AI models. Decart claims that the software can reduce the cost of some neural networks by a hundredfold.

The company hasn’t shared detailed information about how DOS works. However, the blog post in which Decart announced its May funding round did reveal that the platform optimizes AI models by “tuning the kernels.”

Kernels are the basic building blocks of neural networks. They’re relatively simple code snippets designed to run across a large number of chip cores. One common approach to optimizing them, kernel fusion, combines multiple kernels into a single code snippet that uses less hardware. In July, Decart disclosed that a custom model it had developed with DOS uses kernel fusion.

The company says that the platform also includes “proprietary compilers.” AI compilers translate neural networks into the platform-specific programming language of the host chip. They also optimize the models along they way. For example, the compiler that Amazon Web Services offers for its AWS Trainium machine learning chip uses quantization to compress models into a more memory-efficient form.

It’s unclear whether Decart positions DOS as an alternative to the default compilers provided with AI accelerators. According to Amazon, Decart has “worked closely” with its engineers since 2025 to optimize the performance of workloads deployed on its Trainium chips. The newest commercially available iterat

summary.tldr:
Amazon has announced the acquisition of key assets and the technical team from AI startup Decart.AI Inc. for a reported $7.5 billion. The deal includes the hiring of Decart founders Dean Leitersdorf, Moshe Shalev, and Orian Leitersdorf, alongside their research staff. While Amazon did not officially confirm the financial terms, the reported figure represents nearly double the valuation Decart achieved during its May funding round. Anthropic PBC had previously engaged in acquisition talks with Decart for $6 billion before withdrawing in September.

The core of the acquisition is Decart’s 'DOS' platform, a software suite designed to optimize AI model efficiency through kernel tuning and proprietary compilers. Decart claims the platform can reduce neural network costs by up to 100x. The technology utilizes techniques such as kernel fusion—combining multiple neural network code snippets to reduce hardware overhead—and specialized compilers that translate models for specific chip architectures. Amazon intends to integrate this technology to enhance the performance and cost-efficiency of its custom silicon, specifically the AWS Trainium3 chips, which currently deliver 2.52 petaflops of FP8 performance.

Notably, the acquisition excludes Decart’s internally developed AI models, such as the 'Lucy 2.5' and 'Oasis 3' world models, which are designed for low-latency content generation and robotic training data, respectively. Amazon’s integration efforts will focus on optimizing both inference and training workloads, building upon a collaborative relationship between Decart and AWS engineers that began in 2025.
takeaways: **Acquisition Value:** Amazon is reportedly paying $7.5 billion for Decart’s assets and talent, significantly higher than the startup's previous valuation.
**Core Technology:** The 'DOS' platform optimizes AI models via kernel fusion and proprietary compilers, with claims of reducing neural network costs by up to 100x.
**Hardware Integration:** The technology will be applied to AWS Trainium3 chips, which are rated at 2.52 petaflops for FP8 data processing.
**Excluded Assets:** The deal does not include Decart’s proprietary AI models, specifically the Lucy 2.5 and Oasis 3 world models.
**Previous Interest:** Anthropic PBC reportedly attempted to acquire Decart for $6 billion in August before walking away from negotiations in September.

title: Anthropic’s Claude Ship automates the final stage of the software development pipeline
author: Mike Wheatley
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 20:30 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026

Anthropic’s Claude Ship automates the final stage of the software development pipeline

Anthropic PBC isn’t satisfied with having Claude just write new software. With a new update today, Claude now can tell developers when the code it has generated is ready to ship into production environments.

The company announced the launch of Claude Ship , which is a new suite of artificial intelligence agents capable of automating code reviews, bug fixes and approvals. The last one is the most interesting of those capabilities, because code reviews and fixes are nothing new for AI . But Claude’s ability to automatically approve code changes based on the policies predetermined by an organization’s developer team is a novel development that has not been seen before.

Claude Ship is an effort by Anthropic to eliminate the new bottleneck that has emerged in the code review and approval process at companies that have already adopted AI code generation tools. At those organizations, fresh code is being whipped up in double-quick time, and there are also AI agents for checking that code and providing fixes if it’s not working as hoped. But until now, the final review and approval process has always been performed by humans. Claude Ship changes that.

The idea is that human developers can delegate final approval authority to Claude, so now all they really have to do is determine the quality and security standards of the code they’re asking AI to create.

“Most teams want a person to approve every change and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line,” Anthropic said in a blog post. “But a lot of developers build with agents now. On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code and we wanted everything after the pull request to move that fast too.”

Anthropic said Claude Ship consists of three parts. The first is Code Review, which is a tool that has been generally available for some time already. The other two are PR Steward and Claude Approvals, and they’re both still in beta.

PR Steward is designed to handle issues such as failing continuous integration checks, merge conflicts and feedback from Code Review. After each push, it will leave comments on what changes were made and how to roll them back if necessary.

Once PR Steward is done, Claude Approvals takes over. It works by applying an approval policy that’s left

summary.tldr:
Anthropic has launched Claude Ship, a suite of AI agents designed to automate the final stages of the software development lifecycle, specifically code reviews, bug fixes, and production approvals. By allowing developers to delegate final approval authority to Claude based on organization-defined policies, the tool aims to remove the bottleneck created by human-in-the-loop requirements in high-velocity AI-assisted coding environments. The system is intended to accelerate the transition from pull request to production by automating tasks that previously required manual oversight.

Claude Ship consists of three distinct components: the existing Code Review tool, and two new beta features, PR Steward and Claude Approvals. PR Steward manages continuous integration failures, merge conflicts, and feedback implementation, while Claude Approvals executes final sign-offs based on natural language policies stored within the codebase repository. Anthropic recommends that early adopters initially deploy Claude Approvals in an 'observe-only' mode and limit usage to single repositories to mitigate risks associated with automated production deployments.
takeaways: **Component Architecture:** Claude Ship comprises three modules: Code Review (generally available), PR Steward (beta), and Claude Approvals (beta).
**Approval Mechanism:** Claude Approvals functions by reading approval policies defined in natural language files stored directly within the codebase repository.
**Compatibility:** The suite is currently available to Claude Team and Enterprise subscribers and supports integration with GitHub repositories.
**Risk Mitigation:** Anthropic advises users to implement 'observe-only' mode for the beta-stage Claude Approvals and to set monthly spending limits during initial deployment.

title: Anthropic Launches Claude Ship for GitHub Pull Request Review and Fixes
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Anthropic just released Claude Ship . Claude Ship is a set of Anthropic agents that takes GitHub pull requests from review to approval. It bundles 3 agents: Code Review , PR Steward and Claude Approvals . Your GitHub branch rules still decide what merges. TL;DR Size: 3 agents with a local /ship command. Runs on: Anthropic’s cloud for Code Review and PR Steward. /ship runs in the Claude Code CLI locally. Performance: Most Code Reviews finish in 6 to 10 minutes, about 3x faster than the research preview. Best: Claude Code team merged PRs more than doubled from June to September (self-reported). What is Claude Ship? Per the Claude Ship docs , each agent owns 1 step: Code Review looks for logic errors, security vulnerabilities and broken edge cases. Findings land as inline comments, ranked by severity. PR Steward works on failing checks, merge conflicts and review comments. It pushes commits with its fixes. Claude Approvals checks each PR against an approval policy your team writes. Code Review is generally available . The other 2 are in public beta. How does Claude Ship work on a pull request? Code Review finds problems. PR Steward pushes fixes, and a fix can start another review. Claude Approvals then applies your policy. The merge follows your GitHub branch rules. PR Steward is designed not to approve or merge. After each push, it comments on its changes and how to undo them. Developers steer it with @claude and stop it with @claude stop . Claude Approvals reads a policy file at .claude/approvals.yml . Anthropic calls it a smarter CODEOWNERS file. A rule can require 2 people on billing code and 1 on test fixtures. Rules can read PR facts and classifier answers, but not CI results. What does /ship do for developers? Developers run /ship in Claude Code. It commits, pushes and opens the PR. Claude reviews it, then ‘watches’ feedback and failing checks. You merge yourself. Requirements are Claude Code v2.1.330 or later, GitHub CLI 2.63 or later, and git 2.38 or later. A watch ends after 7 days, or on merge or close. /steward skips the review on an open PR. When Claude acts alone, Claude Code blocks merge, approve, auto-merge and force-push commands. Still, a watch uses your own gh and git sign-ins. Claude Ship benchmarks: what has Anthropic reported? Anthropic has published no public benchmark. It shares internal results from its launch post and engineering blog

summary.tldr:
Anthropic has launched Claude Ship, a suite of three specialized agents designed to automate the GitHub pull request lifecycle from initial review to final approval. The system consists of Code Review, which identifies logic errors and security vulnerabilities; PR Steward, which resolves merge conflicts and failing checks by pushing commits; and Claude Approvals, which enforces custom team policies defined in a .claude/approvals.yml file. The tool integrates with the Claude Code CLI, allowing developers to initiate the workflow via a local /ship command.

Performance metrics reported by Anthropic indicate that code reviews typically complete within 6 to 10 minutes, representing a 3x speed improvement over the initial research preview. The system is designed to respect existing GitHub branch protection rules, with PR Steward explicitly restricted from approving or merging code. While Code Review is currently generally available, PR Steward and Claude Approvals remain in public beta. Deployment requires Claude Code v2.1.330, GitHub CLI 2.63, and git 2.38 or later, with the system utilizing the user's local git and GitHub credentials for all operations.
takeaways: **Agent Architecture:** The suite comprises three distinct agents: Code Review (vulnerabilities/logic), PR Steward (fixes/conflicts), and Claude Approvals (policy enforcement).

**Policy Configuration:** Claude Approvals uses a .claude/approvals.yml file, described as a smarter alternative to CODEOWNERS, allowing for granular rules like requiring two reviewers for specific billing-related code.
**CLI Integration:** The /ship command in Claude Code automates the commit, push, and PR opening process, while /steward allows for manual intervention on existing open pull requests.
**Safety Constraints:** When operating autonomously, Claude Code blocks sensitive commands including merge, approve, auto-merge, and force-push to ensure human oversight.
**Performance:** Internal engineering data shows review times of 6 to 10 minutes, with the Claude Code team reporting a doubling of merged PRs between June and September.

title: SpecEngineeringBench: Evaluating Coding Agents as Autonomous Specification Engineers
author: Xingjian Wang, Shijian Wang, Minghao Liu, Ji Zou
contentSnippet:
Authors: Xingjian Wang , Shijian Wang , Minghao Liu , Ji Zou , Zetao Yang , Xinping Lei , Yiming Liang , Shen Yan , Enduo Zhao , Xiaoyang Shen , Weihao Xuan , Jiaheng Liu , Ge Zhang

Abstract: Autonomous specification engineering requires coding agents to translate functional requirements into executable tests and use the results to discover and validate defects. However, existing benchmarks evaluate coding agents on explicitly specified test generation tasks, commonly providing an issue description, a designated test entry point, or files to inspect, leaving the ability to determine what to test and where to investigate insufficiently evaluated. Relying on such clues bypasses the challenge of mapping requirements to implementations and proactively uncovering unknown defects. We propose SpecEngineeringBench, comprising 100 instances from 78 open-source Python repositories across 16 application categories, with multiple recorded defects in each instance. Two independent tasks evaluate complementary capabilities: generating test suites and discovering defects through execution analysis. The evaluation combines test validity, defect detection, and coverage with localization precision and recall. Across seven frontier coding agents, results reveal that test validity and coverage decouple from defect exposure: agents achieve a 91.47% Head Pass Rate and 80.48% Change-focused Coverage alongside a 26.36% Fail-to-Pass Rate, while localization recall drops from 78.11% at the file level to 51.29% at the function level. Autonomous test generation improves file, function, and hunk localization recall by 4.99, 2.77, and 2.69 percentage points over relying solely on existing repository test suites.

Notes: 31 pages, 3figures

summary.tldr:
SpecEngineeringBench is a new evaluation framework designed to test the autonomous capabilities of coding agents in specification engineering, specifically the translation of functional requirements into executable tests and the proactive discovery of defects. Authored by Xingjian Wang et al., the benchmark moves beyond existing standards that provide explicit test entry points or file paths, instead requiring agents to determine what to test and where to investigate within a codebase. The dataset consists of 100 instances sourced from 78 open-source Python repositories across 16 distinct application categories, with each instance containing multiple documented defects.

The benchmark evaluates agents on two primary tasks: generating test suites and discovering defects through execution analysis. Performance is measured via test validity, defect detection, coverage metrics, and localization precision/recall. Testing seven frontier coding agents revealed a significant performance gap: while agents achieved a 91.47% Head Pass Rate and 80.48% Change-focused Coverage, their ability to actually expose defects remained low, with a 26.36% Fail-to-Pass Rate. Furthermore, localization recall demonstrated a sharp decline from 78.11% at the file level to 51.29% at the function level, suggesting that current models struggle with granular defect identification.

Despite these limitations, the study found that autonomous test generation provides a measurable improvement over relying on existing repository test suites. Specifically, the use of autonomous agents increased localization recall by 4.99 percentage points at the file level, 2.77 points at the function level, and 2.69 points at the hunk level. The research, detailed in a 31-page paper, highlights the decoupling of test coverage from actual defect exposure as a critical bottleneck for current autonomous coding agents.
takeaways: **Benchmark Scope:** Comprises 100 instances from 78 open-source Python repositories across 16 application categories.
**Performance Gap:** Agents achieved 80.48% Change-focused Coverage but only a 26.36% Fail-to-Pass Rate, indicating high coverage does not equate to effective defect detection.
**Localization Decay:** Localization recall drops significantly from 78.11% at the file level to 51.29% at the function level.
**Autonomous Advantage:** Autonomous test generation improves localization recall by 4.99% (file), 2.77% (function), and 2.69% (hunk) compared to using existing repository test suites.

title: ReFocus: Progress-Guided Adaptive Practice for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation Reinforcement Learning
author: Haoyuan Li, Wei Huang, Jiehong Lin, Shengrong Zhang
contentSnippet:
Authors: Haoyuan Li , Wei Huang , Jiehong Lin , Shengrong Zhang , Chenzhi Liu , Shengchao Zhou , Hehe Fan , Xiaojuan Qi , Yi Yang

Abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables vision-language-action policies to improve through environmental interaction. However, in long-horizon manipulation, sparse success/failure feedback provides little information about where policies encounter bottlenecks. Moreover, repeated full-task rollouts also leave these bottlenecks weakly analyzed and insufficiently practiced. To this end, we introduce ReFocus, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates between Global and Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. Specifically, during Global RL, we decompose each task into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of subtasks. Then a DAG-based Progress Reward is leveraged for both policy training and bottleneck diagnosis. Based on the identified bottlenecks, ReFocus selects Adaptive Practice Windows, defining task segments from an entry stage to a target stage. It allocates additional interaction to these segments during Local RL while updating the entire policy. After that, it evaluates the policy to perform the full task for the next round of RL, forming an iteration between Global and Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus achieves success rates of 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively, compared with 90.6% and 39.3% for the $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline. Furthermore, we evaluate a real-world adaptation on three long-horizon tasks. On BreadBaker, ReFocus achieves 95% success, compared with 30% for the $\pi_{0.5}$. Project page: this https URL .

Notes: 27 pages, 15 figures

title: Lazy Agents Answer Against Their Own Beliefs: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs Teaches Them to Act on What They Believe
author: Richmond Sin Jing Xuan, Peilin Feng, Wenbin Wang, Soujanya Poria
contentSnippet: AI agents working on long tasks often commit to an answer before they have enough evidence, a behavior called laziness. In our evaluations, they frequently commit even while their stated belief still names several possible answers. An outcome reward at the end of the episode scores only the final answer, so it cannot teach the agent when to commit, because a lucky guess receives the same reward as an answer backed by evidence. During training, however, the simulator can compute the exact posterior over the answer at every step and tell whether the evidence is already enough. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB), which rewards the agent for taking further steps while this posterior still allows several answers and for committing once the evidence is sufficient. The reward needs no judge, critic or reward model, and it never reads the belief line the agent writes before each action. We also introduce Pro Worlds, a benchmark of visual puzzles where the agent views a large world through a small window. We evaluate three vision-language models on three benchmarks, two of which are never seen in training. RLVB improves the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average. Under the outcome reward, GRPO and PPO fall below the base model on average. RLVB also outperforms PPO with a process reward from an LLM judge by 9.3% on average while using 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours. The trained agent answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12% and 74% of the episodes on the three benchmarks, against 8%, 0.4% and 36% for the base model. Its accuracy gain therefore comes from answering more often at high levels of evidence. The belief line shows how the agent reaches this evidence: it acts on its own belief. It commits at only 0.1 to 2.2% of the turns at which the evidence is insufficient and its line still names several answers, against 3 to 68% for the base model.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB), a training framework designed to mitigate 'laziness' in AI agents—a phenomenon where models commit to answers prematurely without sufficient evidence. Unlike standard outcome-based rewards that only score final answers, RLVB utilizes the simulator's ability to compute the exact posterior over potential answers at each step. By rewarding agents for continuing to gather information when the posterior remains ambiguous and for committing only when evidence is sufficient, RLVB eliminates the need for external reward models, judges, or critics.

To evaluate this approach, the authors developed 'Pro Worlds,' a benchmark consisting of visual puzzles where agents navigate a large environment through a restricted window. Testing across three vision-language models and three distinct benchmarks, RLVB demonstrated a 17.1% average performance improvement over base models. Notably, RLVB outperformed PPO with an LLM-based process reward by 9.3% while requiring 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours. The method significantly reduced premature commitment, with agents committing on insufficient evidence in only 0.1% to 2.2% of turns, compared to 3% to 68% for base models, effectively forcing agents to act in alignment with their internal belief states.
takeaways: **Performance Gain:** RLVB improved base model performance by an average of 17.1% across nine distinct settings.
**Efficiency:** The method outperformed PPO with an LLM judge by 9.3% while consuming 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours.
**Commitment Reduction:** Agents trained with RLVB reduced premature commitment on insufficient evidence to a range of 0.1%–2.2%, down from 3%–68% in base models.
**Evidence-Based Accuracy:** The model increased the frequency of answering with sufficient evidence to 51%, 12%, and 74% across the three benchmarks, compared to 8%, 0.4%, and 36% for base models.
**Mechanism:** RLVB functions without a reward model or external judge, relying instead on the simulator's ability to calculate the exact posterior over the answer at each step.

title: Embodied AI Fails the Mirror Test: How a Simple Mirror Breaks Robot Policies
author: Xuanchen Liu, Hejun Zhang, Boxuan Dong, Ying Wu
contentSnippet: Can a simple mirror expose the limitations of today's robotic manipulation policies? Inspired by the mirror self-recognition test in animal cognition, we investigate whether robot policies can reliably manipulate physical objects in scenes containing their reflections. We introduce RoboDojo-Mirror, a benchmark built on RoboDojo that preserves task objectives, success criteria, and policy checkpoints while comparing a mirror-free baseline with single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions. Across five policies spanning Vision-Language-Action models, World Action Models, and agentic policies, every mirror condition reduces aggregate success rates: averaged over the three conditions, the drop ranges from 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points across policies, and it reaches 62.5 points on the mirrored tabletop. Because a mirror is also a physical obstacle, we compare it against geometrically matched non-reflective panels; 50--88\% of mirror-specific failures occur without recorded robot--panel contact, so direct collisions alone do not explain the degradation. Trajectory and contact analyses instead reveal recurring behaviors consistent with phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real ones. Targeted diagnostics further characterize grasping near reflections, policy-dependent pushing progress, and physical-target interaction under main-camera occlusion. Real-robot experiments with π_{0.5} and FastWAM also show lower overall success rates under the upright-mirror and mirrored-tabletop conditions. These findings reveal a shared vulnerability to reflective environments across diverse robot policies and motivate reflection-aware evaluation of embodied intelligence. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/robodojo-mirror.

title: Factorized Context Attention: From Emulated to Native Grid Probing
author: Mohamed Eltahir, Manar Eyad, Yara Alzahrani, Fatimah Albesher
contentSnippet: Models read a book, an hour of video, or an image in one forward pass. As the context grows, this pass slows down, loses accuracy, and stops at the context window. Sparse attention is efficient, but keeps the other two limitations. Grid probing, a recent training-free method, recovers the accuracy and extends the reach by asking a frozen model the same question about short local and strided spans of the input, but every question repeats the whole computation, since each span is encoded again. Our insight is that grid probing is emulated attention, an attention pattern reproduced from outside the model through prompts, since each probe only restricts which part of the input the question can see. We introduce Factorized Context Attention (FCA), a training-free block-sparse attention that runs the same pattern natively, as the attention of the model itself. FCA encodes the input once into a KV cache, reads all spans as masked sequences in one batched forward, and uses a stair position schedule to keep every span inside the trained position range. Across long video understanding, long-context text inference and image grounding, FCA matches the accuracy and the reach of grid probing at a fraction of its cost. It gains about 10 points over the single pass on long video and 9 to 14 points on long novels, finds needles in videos of over a thousand frames and in texts four times the length of the window, and answers a later question about the same input in as little as a tenth of the time of grid probing. Native attention thus keeps what emulated attention gains without its cost, all with existing frozen language and vision-language models.

title: VenusOCR2.0: Towards Efficient and Effective Document Parsing
author: Lei Li, Zheng Wei, Yi Yuan, Qingbin Liu
contentSnippet: We present VenusOCR2.0, a compact 1B-parameter vision-language recognizer designed for both high-accuracy and high-throughput document parsing across text, tables, and formulas. To continuously improve recognition quality without self-training collapse, we build a bounded recursive self-improvement (RSI) data engine where the model acts strictly as a weakness probe, while external multi-expert medoid consensus, VLM visual verification, and factorized synthesis supply reliable supervision across pretraining, curated SFT, and RLVR. VenusOCR2.0 couples a dynamic-resolution SigLIP2 encoder and 2x2 spatial token merging with a Qwen3-0.6B decoder, adopting compact atomic OTSL tokens to shorten table sequences and reduce structural errors. To further eliminate the autoregressive decoding bottleneck, we introduce PTPv2, a lightweight (sim67M) decoupled parallel draft module that combines frozen multi-layer verifier conditioning, a standalone learned mask, and block-causal all-position next-token prediction. On OmniDocBenchv1.6, VenusOCR2.0 achieves an overall score of 96.45 and a state-of-the-art 98.57 formula CDM, substantially outperforming massive general-purpose VLMs such as Gemini-3-Pro (92.91) and Qwen3-VL-235B (89.78). title: Reinforcing Diffusion Models by Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching
author: Yihong Luo
contentSnippet: Forward diffusion reinforcement learning (RL)---enabling deterministic ODE sampling without trajectory backpropagation---has grown increasingly popular for efficiently aligning diffusion models. However, we reveal that existing methods essentially rely on signed reward-weighted regression (RWR), regressing the trainable policy velocity onto rollouts from a behavior distribution. Unbiased baseline subtraction implicitly assumes that the policy velocity equals the behavior marginal velocity---an idealized assumption violated under classifier-free guidance (CFG) rollouts, offline/off-policy updates, and imperfect online self-consistency. This behavior--policy mismatch breaks baseline invariance and injects baseline-induced gradient drift, destabilizing training. To resolve this issue, we propose Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching (iTDM), taking the infinitesimal limit of Trajectory Distribution Matching toward a time-local reward-guided target via the posterior-score identity to yield a sample-level gradient anchored at the behavior velocity without learning an additional reward-tilted target score. Tracking this velocity with an online auxiliary denoiser guarantees exact baseline invariance at the auxiliary optimum, effectively suppressing baseline drift across both online and offline RL. Extensive experiments across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment show that iTDM achieves state-of-the-art in-domain and out-of-domain performance across group-wise online/offline RL and pairwise offline RL. Notably, on the challenging GenEval2 benchmark, iTDM converges nearly 3\times faster than competing methods while scaling smoothly to 0.87 without collapse. Furthermore, iTDM scales effectively to the 5.6B FLUX.3 model, achieving better performance across both in-domain and unseen metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/Luo-Yihong/iTDM

title: ThinkMorph-SSL: Scaling Interleaved Multimodal Reasoning with Pretext Tasks
author: Jiawei Gu, Linjie Li, Yiming Liu, Yunzhuo Hao
contentSnippet: People reason with pictures as well as words. Interleaved multimodal reasoning gives models a similar way to solve problems by creating intermediate images and using them to guide further reasoning. Training models with this ability usually relies on task-specific demonstrations, which are difficult to collect. We introduce ThinkMorph-SSL, a two-stage training recipe that uses images themselves as a source of supervision. The first stage, pretext reasoning, converts visual pretext tasks, such as image colorization and denoising, into instruction-free interleaved traces. Models describe a corrupted or transformed image, generate a restored or canonical image, and interpret the result. The second stage uses automatically constructed demonstrations for question-driven instruction tuning. At the same instruction-tuning budget, models trained with pretext reasoning outperform those trained with instruction tuning alone. The full recipe improves over the base model by an average of 11.33 accuracy points across twelve benchmarks. These results show that supervision derived from images can build the visual skills needed for interleaved reasoning and improve learning from task-specific demonstrations.

title: Qwen-Image-HD: Autoregressive Diffusion for High Definition Image Generation
author: Zihao Liu, Zekai Zhang, Shengming Yin, Zikai Zhou
contentSnippet: Fine-tuning a generator on a complete high-resolution canvas requires long image sequences and substantial computation, yet local regions can still exhibit unnatural repetitive stripes when training resources are limited. We introduce Qwen-Image-HD, which adapts Qwen-Image 2.0 to high-resolution synthesis through local training and blockwise autoregressive generation. Each prediction covers a target tile at 1K scale, conditioned on high-resolution upper and left neighbors and a compressed historical thumbnail. These conditions provide adjacent fine-scale structures and an overview of the scene generated so far. To integrate these complementary cues, we map both forms of history and the target to a shared canvas coordinate system to express their spatial relationships and scale differences. On Qwen-Image-Bench at 4K, Qwen-Image-HD achieves stronger overall evaluation performance than direct 4K generation with FLUX-3-Image-Klein. Compared with full-image 4K supervised fine-tuning of the same backbone, it achieves better generation quality with lower training compute and higher inference efficiency, while exhibiting fewer unnatural repetitive stripes in original-resolution comparisons. We further introduce a Wavefront-AutoRegressive inference schedule that generates tiles on the same anti-diagonal concurrently across GPUs to reduce single-image latency.

title: Residual Guidance for Real-Time Interactive Video Generation
author: NaHyeon Park, Kyeong-Hwan Moon, Youjin Jeon, Hyunjung Shim
contentSnippet: Real-time interactive video generation allows users to change the prompt during generation to steer the evolving video. However, existing streaming models, which generate videos chunk by chunk, often keep following the previous prompt after a switch. We trace this failure to context inertia, where the previous chunk acts as a strong prior that suppresses the new prompt. Furthermore, we find that this inertia persists even when the cache retains only the previous chunk, yet discarding the context breaks visual continuity, which limits approaches that edit the cache. Rather than editing the cache, we propose Residual Guidance (RG), a simple, training-free method that counteracts context inertia with a correction measured outside the cache. Specifically, RG denoises the re-noised previous chunk once under the new prompt without the cache and adds the resulting residual to the early denoising steps of the next chunk, where its content is largely decided and the new prompt is most suppressed. Across settings ranging from a single switch to long multi-switch generation, RG substantially improves prompt switching capability on existing streaming models, including those with dedicated switching mechanisms, while largely retaining visual quality. As it requires no training or per-model tuning and adds only one forward pass per chunk, RG can be easily integrated into existing real-time video generation pipelines.

title: RoMo Hands: A Large Scale Richly Organized Text to Hand Motion Dataset
author: Yizhak Ben-Shabat, Jiahao Zhang, Joseph Liu, Seonghyeon Moon
contentSnippet: While text-driven body motion generation has matured, pure-hand synthesis remains bottlenecked by data. Existing datasets often treat hands as rigid end-effectors, lack fine-grained captions, or are too limited in scale to support robust generalization. We introduce RoMo Hands, an in-the-wild, text-paired dataset of ~542K sequences (884 hours, 95.5M frames at 30 fps) which is an order of magnitude larger than prior work. To ensure high-quality supervision, a stringent dexterity filter discards low-articulation sequences, focusing the distribution on complex bimanual movement. Each clip is paired with five captions at increasing granularities from global semantic tags to atomic finger states, organized under a hierarchical taxonomy. To bridge the gap between body and hand architectures, we propose a novel 393-D bimanual representation that adapts redundant body-motion paradigms to the high-DoF kinematics of hands. Systematic benchmarking of diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive generators reveals distinct trade-offs under these hand-specific adaptations, including a sharp divergence between semantic alignment and kinematic plausibility. Our dataset, representation, and benchmark establish a rigorous foundation for the next generation of dexterous motion synthesis. Project page: https://romodataset.github.io/romo-hands/.
