title: AWS is making AI agents more decisive and secure with its latest Strands updates
author: Mike Wheatley
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 13:00 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026

AWS is making AI agents more decisive and secure with its latest Strands updates

Amazon Web Services Inc. is trying to tackle two major headaches for artificial intelligence agents developers with a major update to Strands Agents, its open-source toolkit for building autonomous workers.

Today, the cloud infrastructure giant unveiled a new family of open-weight “decision models” called Strands Decider v2, along with the debut of Box CLI, bringing native sandbox support for popular coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Kiro CLI.

AWS introduced Strands Agents back in May 2025, and recently the project has emerged as the centerpiece of the company’s agentic development strategy. Strands Agents is a software development kit that gives developers a flexible, model-driven foundation for connecting large language models to enterprise data and tools.

After introducing Strands Harness , which allows Strands agents to be deployed in any computing environment, in September, AWS followed up with Strands Decider one month later. Unlike regular LLMs that focus on text outputs, Strands Decider is a category of decision models designed to evaluate scenarios and assign probability scores to a predetermined list of choices. At the time, AWS said decision models can help to improve the efficiency of AI agent workflows, such as routing support tickets or choosing which software tool to invoke to complete a given task.

More decisive agents

With Strands Decider v2, AWS is adding five even more capable decision models to its lineup. The open-weight models are built on Google LLC’s Gemma 4 architecture and they’re available in various sizes, ranging from a lightweight edge version to a beefy 31 billion-parameter variant for complex decision-making. In a blog post, AWS explained that the new models provide greater accuracy across text, image and video tasks, and deliver more optimal confidence scores, so agents can better determine when it’s OK to take an action or escalate to a human decision-maker.

The Strands Decider v2 models have also been given the ability to process longer inputs, including multistep agent execution logs, so they can collaborate with other agents.

title: Aevius Labs launches with $22M to bring understandable intelligence to medical data
author: Kyt Dotson
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 12:40 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026

Aevius Labs launches with $22M to bring understandable intelligence to medical data

Boston-based Aevius Labs Inc. , a clinical medical data company, today announced it has raised $22 million in funding led by Insight Partners to build and train artificial intelligence foundation models that can understand and query unstructured medical text, imaging and other data.

A spinout of Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, the company develops AI models that turn information from healthcare, payer, and life sciences organizations into insights other AI tools can act on. The company said it wants to provide a foundational “brain” that can take notes, medical artifacts, clinicians’ transcriptions, lab work, radiology imaging, electronic health record information and other specialty medical data, and make it more accessible to healthcare workers.

The platform can take all this information and use it to represent the whole patient, their medical experience, population studies and actionable insights for clinicians and doctors in the language that they speak. The company said it’s designed to support applications spanning healthcare delivery, operations, and life sciences.

The company was founded by key members of Modella AI Inc., which was acquired by pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca PLC , using the company’s AI model and agent development for oncology research.

“Our mission is to make medicine computable,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Rowland Pettit, M.D., Ph.D. “As a physician-scientist, I’ve worked across many types of clinical data, and there is far more knowledge in those records than we’re able to use today.”

The company said its models learn relationships across different forms of medical data and throughout a patient’s history. It does this by building a dynamic, refreshable representation of the patient, essentially a computable picture of the patient and their entire medical clinical state and trajectory that the doctor or clinician can interact with. An organization can use this to build tools to forecast outcomes, identify changes and monitor outcomes over time.

title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
author: James O'Donnell
contentSnippet: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.  Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.  This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll , 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).  But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place. Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is , Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer. You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. The company argues that as model capabilities increase, the probability of achieving moral significance rises, necessitating stricter internal safety protocols and ethical constraints to prevent potential harm to these systems. This stance aligns with a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, where 39% indicated that future AI systems would likely possess consciousness, and public sentiment, where 33% of US respondents believe AI will eventually develop consciousness.

title: Supercharging transformer residual connections
author: Google AI Research Blog
contentSnippet:
November 23, 2026 Kyriakos Axiotis, Staff Research Scientist, and Thomas Fu, Principal Engineer, Google Research

We present DeepCrossAttention (DCA), an architecture that enhances transformer networks by using learnable weights and depth-wise cross-attention to dynamically combine outputs from previous layers, preventing the information dilution seen in traditional residual connections. Presented in our ICML 2025 paper, this architectural improvement allows models to achieve the same quality up to three times faster with a negligible increase in parameters.

Think of a traditional deep learning model like a giant game of "Telephone": data passes through layer after layer, with each layer changing the information slightly. If a network has dozens or hundreds of layers, the original learning signal can become severely degraded or lost by the time it reaches all layers, which is known as the vanishing gradient problem in AI.

To overcome this challenge and enable the training of networks with dozens or hundreds of layers, transformers rely heavily on residual connections , also known as “skip” connections, which act like an information highway or a shortcut. Instead of forcing the data to pass exclusively through the complicated layer, a duplicate copy of the original input skips right past this layer and is added directly to its output. This ensures that the model always has the original raw data to refer back to.

The standard residual connection implements a simple operation: point-wise summation of a layer's output with its input. While computationally efficient, this simple process has a key limitation: it treats all prior representations with equal weight, leading to information dilution in deep networks. As features propagate through many layers, specific, high-resolution details from earlier layers can be averaged out or distorted, making it difficult for the network to selectively retrieve them. This forces the network to recompute them, reducing learning efficiency.

In our ICML 2025 paper, "DeepCrossAttention: Supercharging Transformer Residual Connections ," we studied the shortcomings of the traditional residual architecture and introduced DeepCrossAttention (DCA), which generalizes residual connections by allowing each layer to dynamically select and route features from the history of preceding layers. By allowing the model to dynamically choose

summary.tldr:
Google Research scientists Kyriakos Axiotis and Thomas Fu have introduced DeepCrossAttention (DCA), an architectural modification for transformer networks designed to mitigate information dilution caused by traditional residual connections. Presented at ICML 2025, DCA replaces standard point-wise additive skip connections with a dynamic routing mechanism. This allows models to selectively retrieve and combine features from the history of preceding layers on a per-token basis, rather than relying on rigid, equal-weight summation. The architecture utilizes two primary mechanisms: dynamic layer routing, which computes mixing weights via input-dependent projections, and depth-wise cross-attention, which queries prior layer embeddings without the computational overhead of standard sequence-based attention.

Empirical testing on the LM1B and C4 datasets demonstrates that DCA achieves performance parity with standard transformers in up to five times fewer training steps. In specific benchmarks, a 30-layer DCA model outperformed a 42-layer standard transformer, representing a 29% reduction in depth and parameter count. The architecture adds less than 0.2% to the total model parameter count and can be retrofitted onto pre-trained models; in such cases, continued training with DCA reduced perplexity on LM1B by 0.19, compared to 0.02 for standard continued training. The research also contrasts DCA with hyper-connections and manifold-constrained hyper-connections, noting that DCA avoids the training instabilities associated with unconstrained mixing matrices.
takeaways: **Performance Efficiency:** DCA achieves target perplexity levels with 29% fewer layers and parameters compared to standard transformer architectures.
**Training Speed:** Models utilizing DCA reach performance benchmarks up to five times faster than standard residual-based transformers.
**Parameter Overhead:** The DCA mechanism adds less than 0.2% to the total model parameter count, maintaining a negligible memory and compute footprint.
**Retrofitting Capability:** DCA can be applied to existing pre-trained models, yielding a 0.19 perplexity reduction on LM1B during continued training compared to 0.02 for standard methods.
**Architectural Innovation:** DCA replaces additive point-wise connections with depth-wise cross-attention, allowing for dynamic, token-specific routing of historical layer information.

title: RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation
author: Hugging Face Blog
contentSnippet:
🤖 Models | 📄 Tech Report | 📊 Data | 💻 Code | 🌐 Project Page | 📈 Benchmark

Deploying robots in real-world settings requires reliable perception throughout an interaction. To pick something up, a robot needs to follow the positions of its gripper and the object as they move. In a laboratory, a robot handling a pipette must keep track of its tip while aligning it with the opening of a tube. These tasks become harder when nearby objects clutter the view, the gripper obscures the object being handled, or the viewing angle changes.

One way to help robots follow these interactions is to track specific locations on the objects they handle. This is the idea behind point tracking . Given a location in one video frame, a tracker estimates where that same point appears in subsequent frames, when it is occluded, and where it reappears. These trajectories can help robots learn from demonstrations, plan and guide movements, and model how objects respond to actions.

Robotics systems often rely on off-the-shelf trackers to automatically annotate motion in videos and provide feedback during execution. And current trackers score well on established robotics benchmarks, suggesting they could be ready for wider use in real-world systems. We wanted to see whether those results hold up across the varied scenes, viewpoints, and object interactions robots encounter in practice.

We introduce RoboTrack , a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. RoboTrack-Bench contains 307 human-annotated videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2 , and EgoVerse, covering different robots and human hands, cluttered scenes, and first- and third-person viewpoints. To study how training data affects tracking in these settings, we also extend MolmoSpaces , Ai2’s simulation ecosystem for robot learning, to generate dense point tracks from simulated robot manipulation trajectories. This pipeline produces RoboTrack-15M , a new synthetic training dataset targeted toward robotic manipulation.

Training with this simulated data improves tracking on real manipulation footage. RoboTrack-Bench (top-right) provides human-annotated point tracks in real manipulation videos.

title: CocoonBench: Can Multilingual Search Agents Escape Language Information Cocoons?
author: Hongchuan Zeng
contentSnippet: Multilingual search agents can access the global Web, yet may remain trapped in a language environment with insufficient evidence; we refer to this failure as a language information cocoon. However, existing search benchmarks largely operate within a single language, especially English, overlooking entity connections across multiple languages. We introduce CocoonBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether multilingual search agents can escape such language information cocoons. CocoonBench mines answer-centered relational paths from a frozen Wikidata-derived graph and selects clue sets that are individually necessary and jointly identify a unique answer. Using language-specific entity names, it records each task's minimum language cover, removes direct identifiers, and renders each task as matched prompts in three languages together with its construction certificate and provenance. Across 10 state-of-the-art models, mean accuracy on CocoonBench ranges from 33.8% (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) to 69.7% (Claude-Opus-4.8), leaving even the strongest system below 70%. The same construction certificates support path-aligned trajectory analysis, enabling diagnosis of model failures in language routing, evidence-path recovery, and answer use. The result shows that escaping a language cocoon requires more than switching languages: successful cross-lingual search depends on both covering the correct languages and connecting the evidence found across them.

title: WeMM-Ecom: Advancing Multimodal Content Understanding for WeChat E-Commerce
author: Binhui Xie
contentSnippet: We present WeMM-Ecom, a family of multimodal large language models that deliver frontier e-commerce capabilities while achieving state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at their respective scales. The family spans five sizes, from a 0.8B dense model to a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. Our training pipeline begins with two-stage continued pre-training that progressively raises the proportion of e-commerce data within a diverse multimodal data mixture, followed by hybrid-thinking post-training that combines on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning to support both non-thinking and thinking modes. For evaluation, we construct a comprehensive suite of 28 e-commerce benchmarks (23 in-house and five open-source) covering eight business scenarios and complement it with 64 public general-purpose benchmarks. On the e-commerce suite, WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B surpasses substantially larger open-source flagship models, including Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, HY4, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. On the general-purpose suite, every WeMM-Ecom model surpasses its similarly sized Qwen3.5 counterpart, with the lightweight variants (e.g., WeMM-Ecom-2B) showing clear advantages over leading lightweight models such as Qwen3.5-2B, MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B, and LFM3-VL-2B. Beyond benchmarks, WeMM-Ecom now powers hundreds of production use cases in WeChat, including catalog management, multimodal product search, and livestream commerce, serving billion-scale requests per day. We publicly release all model weights and detail our data curation, training recipe, and benchmark construction to facilitate future work on domain-specialized multimodal models. We have released the model weights and code to facilitate future research at https://github.com/Tencent/WeMM-Ecom.

title: Does the Mixer Matter ? Paired-Seed Ablations of Tiny Bilingual Language Models
author: Ayoub Kirouane
contentSnippet: We report paired-seed architecture ablations from the development of Sophea Artemis, our in-house Greek-English model family. Every arm trains on the same 3B targets with a shared tokenizer and recipe; models range from 54M to 759M total parameters and roughly 54M to 124M active parameters. The main finding is that, at this tiny scale, stored capacity matters far more than mixer design. On a fixed held-out test, replacing the dense feed-forward blocks of a recurrent/attention hybrid with sixteen routed experts, at nearly the same approximate active parameters, lowers loss by 0.079 (Greek) and 0.112 (English) nats per target, and doubling to 32 experts lowers it by a further 0.022 and 0.031, at every paired seed. Reusing a four-layer block three times recovers about 40-44% of the gap between a shallow and an independently deep model, consistent with looped-Transformer results. In contrast, the choice among grouped-query attention (GQA), Gated DeltaNet (GDN) hybrids and a Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) hybrid moves loss by only about 0.01-0.02 nats; a 1:1 GDN/GQA hybrid is the one dense variant that improves on GQA in both languages at every held-out seed. In bits per character, Greek and English held-out losses are similar despite a 74.49%/25.51% training split, and synthetic mathematics, which comes from a collection outside the training sources, is the hardest Greek test component and gains least from added experts. Cached decoding needs its own qualification: trained models passed cached-versus-full logit checks only under a fixed-reduction inference policy, which itself changes 1.4-2.8% of next-token argmax choices relative to native evaluation. All results are conditional on one recipe and scale.

title: GC-MoE K3: A Green-Context Role Graph for Latent Mixture-of-Experts Decode
author: Yong Li
contentSnippet: Kimi K3 combines a latent routed mixture of experts with full-width shared experts. A complete feed-forward evaluation must score and select experts, project tokens into the latent space, exchange tokens across expert-parallel ranks, compute the routed and shared branches, and normalize and project the routed sum before joining the branches. We present GC-MoE K3, a datacenter Blackwell implementation that schedules this entire evaluation as a CUDA Graph across two Green Contexts. Five base roles split input projection, routing, dispatch, expert computation, and finalization. Dispatch can fill the routed input ring while the compute partition evaluates shared experts. Finalize waits for the expert owners needed by each token and overlaps routed reduction and RMSNorm with loading the output projection weights. Conditional roles reuse the communication partition for routed computation and reduce split-$K$ projection partials. On GB200 at EP8, EP16, and EP32, the operator is faster at all 24 measured configurations than the paired SGLang-style reference (mean speedup $1.1324\times$). A comparison with historical vLLM-style measurements gives $1.3651\times$ across the same 24 shapes. Both latency comparisons time single-layer graph replay on synthetic K3-shaped inputs with a residual prefix. The separate paired numerical suite passes all 142 cases and 2,936 rank checks.

author: Jess Weatherbed
contentSnippet: Muse can find Walmart’s Black Friday deals so that you don’t have to. | Image: Walmart Walmart will now let Meta's Muse shop on your behalf, allowing the AI agent to find and purchase Black Friday deals via Walmart's Sparky AI assistant. title: 27 Cybersecurity Terms to Prepare You for the Age of AI
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: AI now sits on both sides of the security fight, and the vocabulary has changed with it. IBM’s 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report found that 1 in 4 malicious breaches were AI-enabled, up 56% year over year. Those breaches cost an average of $6 million, about $1 million above the $4.99 million global average. Attackers now target the models themselves, the agents that act on their output, and the people who trust what AI produces. The reference lists have moved fast to keep up. OWASP published its Top 10 for LLM Applications 2026 on August 4, 2026, and its first Top 10 for Agentic Applications in December 2025. MITRE ATLAS maps attacker tactics against AI systems the way ATT&CK does for IT. The 27 terms below are grouped in 4 parts: attacks on models, agentic risks, AI-powered attacks on people, and the defenses that answer them. Part 1: Attacks on the model itself These attacks target what a model reads, learns or reveals. NIST groups them into evasion, poisoning, privacy and misuse in its Adversarial Machine Learning taxonomy (NIST AI 100-2e2025) , published March 2025. 1. Prompt injection Prompt injection is input crafted to override a model’s intended instructions. It has ranked No. 1 on every edition of the OWASP LLM list, including the 2026 edition . LLMs have no hard boundary between instructions and data, so any text the model reads can try to steer it. 2. Indirect prompt injection Indirect prompt injection hides the malicious instruction in content the model retrieves: an email, a web page, a PDF or a code comment. The user never types it. The clearest real case is EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) , a zero-click flaw in Microsoft 365 Copilot rated CVSS 9.3. Aim Security showed that one crafted email could make Copilot leak organizational data; Microsoft fixed it server-side in May 2025. 3. Jailbreak A jailbreak tricks a model into ignoring its safety training, usually through role-play, fake context or sheer volume. Anthropic’s many-shot jailbreaking research showed that stuffing a long prompt with up to 256 fake dialogues can override safety behavior. Its effectiveness grows with context window size, following a power law. 4. Data poisoning Data poisoning plants malicious samples in training or fine-tuning data so the model learns harmful behavior. title: Architect Labs Unveils Frostbite, an Interaction Net CPU Designed by AI
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Architect Labs has introduced Frostbite , an AI-designed CPU with a new instruction set built around interaction nets. The company states that its AI agents designed Frostbite from interaction net theory down to final GDS. In pre-silicon tests, it reports 4.59x the performance per watt of a modern in-order CPU core. TL;DR Size: 1 quad (2×2 tiles) plus 4 L3 nodes takes 0.792 mm² on 7 nm. No parameter count (it is a CPU). Runs on: Pre-silicon only. Final GDS closes at 500 MHz on 7 nm. An FPGA-hosted playground is planned. Performance: 4.59x perf per watt (geomean, 25 workloads) and 8.77x perf per area vs 1 in-order core. Best: 23.12x perf per watt on conv2d. What is Frostbite? Frostbite is a CPU from Architect Labs that executes programs as interaction nets in hardware. Programs are written in Vine , a Rust-like language, and compiled to an IR called Ivy. The chip is a mesh of tiles, each with its own small local memory. The launch post on X states that the AI agents co-designed the ISA and chip architecture given only interaction net theory. How do interaction nets enable parallelism? Interaction nets were introduced by Yves Lafont at POPL 1990 . A program is a graph of nodes. Computation rewrites pairs of nodes connected through their ports. Each node has 1 principal port, so active pairs never overlap and can fire in any order. Every value is used exactly once, so there is no shared mutable state to guard. A 5-queens net has 3,183 interactions and a 262-step critical path. About 12 interactions are ready per step. Software runtimes such as HVM2 already run interaction nets on GPUs. Frostbite moves the model into the ISA itself. How is the Frostbite hardware organized? The chip is built from tiles grouped into 2×2 quads. Each tile has front end, engine, memory and system blocks. A runtime domain adds a frame manager, scheduler, work queue and outlet. Its ISA adds wide bundles, hardware loop counters, streams, and ops that take, peek or copy values. Each tile runs its own queued work first. If idle, it takes work from a neighbor. If none is found, it goes inactive to save power. The company says this work stealing emerged during design and was not hand-specified. How did AI agents design the chip? Agents first synthesized papers and built Python models. Their output was a 141-page PDF. It was deleted after the first RTL pass because its estimates were physica

Architect Labs has introduced Frostbite , an AI-designed CPU with a new instruction set built around interaction nets. The company states that its AI agents designed Frostbite from interaction net theory down to final GDS. In pre-silicon tests, it reports 4.59x the performance per watt of a modern in-order CPU core.

TL;DR Size: 1 quad (2×2 tiles) plus 4 L3 nodes takes 0.792 mm² on 7 nm. No parameter count (it is a CPU). Runs on: Pre-silicon only.

An FPGA-hosted playground is planned.

title: Meta TLX Brings Warp-Group GPU Control to Triton on Hopper, Blackwell, AMD
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Meta has published a detailed report on TLX (Triton Low-Level Extensions) . It is the GPU compiler extension behind Meta’s production ML kernels. Meta TLX is a Triton extension that exposes warp groups, barriers, TMA and clusters to Python kernels. It targets NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell plus AMD MI300 and MI350-series GPUs. For kernel engineers, the message is CUDA-level control without leaving Triton. TL;DR What it is: an extension to Triton, not a new language. A Blackwell GEMM takes roughly 200 lines of Python-level Triton . Runs on: NVIDIA Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200, GB200), AMD MI300 and MI350-series. MIT-licensed. Performance: within -0.9% to +3.7% of cuBLAS on 6 H100 FP16 GEMM shapes ( PyTorch ). Best: a 4x speedup on an H100 linear compression kernel for ads inference ( Meta ). Worst: dense LLM-style attention forward reaches about 87% of FlashAttention-4 on B200 ( PyTorch ). Bottom line: Best: hand-tuned performance from short Triton code. Worst: all numbers are self-reported, with no independent benchmarks yet. What is TLX and what problem does it solve? Triton programs GPUs at the block level. CUDA programs them at the thread level. Modern GPUs need something in between. Hopper introduced warp specialization and the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA). Blackwell added tensor memory (TMEM), cluster execution and paired-CTA execution. Meta says CUDA could express these patterns, but only with large amounts of architecture-specific code. TLX fills that gap with a model the research team calls MIMW (Multi-Instruction, Multi-Warp) . The warp group becomes the basic unit of orchestration. Triton still defines what runs. TLX defines how it is orchestrated. Engineers write ordinary Triton and add TLX calls only where control matters. How does TLX work? TLX adds 5 extension areas on top of Triton: Warp-group orchestration: warp groups get roles such as producer, consumer and epilogue. Synchronization: warp groups sync through hardware mbarriers. Thread-level sync stays with the compiler. Memory orchestration: direct access to TMA, asynchronous tensor-core ops and TMEM. Cluster execution: multiple CTAs cooperate through distributed shared memory and cluster-wide barriers. Optional layouts: the compiler infers layouts. Programmers override them only for speed. The API reads like Triton. Meta’s Blackwell matmul example uses tlx.local_alloc , tlx.alloc_barr

summary.tldr:
Meta has released TLX (Triton Low-Level Extensions), an MIT-licensed extension for the Triton compiler designed to provide CUDA-level hardware control while maintaining Python-based kernel development. TLX targets NVIDIA Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200, GB200) architectures, as well as AMD MI300 and MI350-series GPUs. By introducing a Multi-Instruction, Multi-Warp (MIMW) programming model, TLX allows engineers to orchestrate warp groups, hardware barriers, the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA), and cluster execution without the verbosity of raw CUDA, effectively bridging the gap between block-level Triton abstractions and thread-level hardware capabilities.

Technically, TLX functions as an orchestration layer where the warp group serves as the primary unit of execution. It introduces five specific extension areas: warp-group orchestration (producer/consumer/epilogue roles), hardware-level mbarriers for synchronization, direct TMA and asynchronous tensor-core operations, cluster-wide shared memory management, and manual layout overrides. Meta reports that a Blackwell GEMM can be implemented in approximately 200 lines of Python-based Triton code. Performance benchmarks on six H100 FP16 GEMM shapes show results ranging from -0.9% to +3.7% compared to cuBLAS, while specific internal use cases, such as an H100 linear compression kernel for ads inference, achieved a 4x speedup. Conversely, dense LLM-style attention forward passes on B200 hardware currently reach approximately 87% of FlashAttention-4 performance.
takeaways: **Architecture Support:** Compatible with NVIDIA Hopper (H100), Blackwell (B200, GB200), and AMD MI300/MI350-series GPUs.
**Performance Metrics:** Achieved -0.9% to +3.7% performance parity with cuBLAS on H100 FP16 GEMM shapes and a 4x speedup on specific ads inference linear compression kernels.
**Programming Model:** Implements a Multi-Instruction, Multi-Warp (MIMW) model where warp groups act as the primary unit of orchestration, utilizing hardware mbarriers for synchronization.
**Key Features:** Adds five extension areas to Triton, including direct TMA access, cluster execution, and explicit warp-group role assignment (producer, consumer, epilogue).
**Caveats:** All performance data is self-reported by Meta with no independent third-party benchmarking currently available.

title: When Does Optical Context Compression Pay Off? A Decode-Aware Cost Analysis of Reasoning VLMs
author: Ziqing Ge
contentSnippet: Rendering long text as images lets a vision-language model (VLM) read a document with fewer input tokens, and evaluations often count mainly these prefill tokens. We show that for reasoning models this accounting is incomplete. Across five models and two long-context benchmarks, reading the rendered document makes the model think longer: decode length grows by 1.5-3.5x on the four general-purpose VLMs tested, and under typical output pricing this decode tax makes image input more expensive than text for two of the five models on QuALITY. Unrecoverable information loss is not sufficient to explain the tax at moderate compression: Qwen's OCR of the same images recovers 98.7% of words, and feeding Kimi-K3 its own transcription as text restores text-mode reasoning length and accuracy. Whether compression pays off reduces to an exchange rate, (1-1/c)/(r-1), that must exceed the workload's price-weighted ratio of output to input tokens; this accounting decomposition shows why Kimi-K3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash can benefit and Qwen and GLM cannot. None of the training-free signals we test predicts the tax before generation. As a practical heuristic, an image-first policy that sends only inputs with a per-input compression ratio of at least 1.6 to images and falls back to text once image-mode reasoning costs as much as the input's prefill saving cuts the bill by 6-14% on Kimi-K3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at an accuracy cost of 0.3-1.2 points; on QuALITY, asking for a reasoning budget on both paths is a stronger lever.

title: Grokking as a Subspace Search: Computing the Destination Before Training
author: Sunjae Jeong
contentSnippet: Grokking is the phenomenon in which a neural network generalizes long after it has memorized its training data. Many explanations have been proposed for the delay between memorization and generalization. However, none of them can say before training where the network is heading, so they cannot be tested against one another. We show that on group tasks this destination can be computed from the task itself before training begins. It is a low-dimensional subspace of the network's embeddings, which we call the right subspace, and we prove that it is essentially unique. Knowing the destination makes our hypothesis falsifiable: the delay is a search for the right subspace, and generalization begins when the network finds it. When we give the network the right subspace from the start, the delay disappears. When we take the right subspace away, accuracy stops at a ceiling that we compute before training, and on multiplication the network cannot generalize at all. When we train the network normally, its embeddings move toward the right subspace by themselves, long before test accuracy rises. Finally, interventions during training show that this search sets the length of the delay, and that noise in the optimization does not. On every group task that we tested, grokking is a search for the right subspace, and the delay is the time that this search takes.

We show that on group tasks this destination can be computed from the task itself before training begins. title: Post-Training Agents for Long-Document Reasoning
author: Sushant Mehta
contentSnippet: Professional documents are a long-context workload that retrieval-style benchmarks do not capture. In a ten-domain enterprise collection, a task's evidence is spread across a source document of median length 27 pages (mean 48.8, maximum 873); a third of tasks rest mainly on charts, drawings, and maps; and 70.9% require two or more reasoning hops. We post-train Kimi-K2.7, an open-weight foundation model, at its full context window on 1,465 expert-authored tasks with atomic rubrics from that collection, training rank-32 adapters with one round of privileged-context on-policy self-distillation followed by two rounds of rubric-reward reinforcement learning. We render each PDF as text for training and as extracted text plus selected page images at evaluation. The smoothed RL training reward rises from 0.37 in the first tenth of the run to 0.67 in the last. On the 100-task GDP.pdf holdout, served in a 262,144-token window, strict pass (all rubric criteria met) more than doubles after the second round, from 11.0% to 24.5%, with gains across input lengths up to 240K tokens. Mean tokens generated stay flat (9,803 to 9,733), so the gain does not come from longer outputs. GPT-5.6 Sol's leaderboard strict pass is 30.7% at a measured 3,422 tokens. On 220 out-of-domain GDPval tasks, where the model runs as a long-horizon tool-using agent, mean rubric reward rises from 0.571 to 0.746 after the third round and zero-credit tasks fall from 54 to 10, while messages per task fall 18%, from 70.9 to 58.2. In paired trajectories, the third round replaces a context-thrashing retry loop with one up-front check of all sources, and verification extends from checking that files exist to checking what they contain. We argue that long-context evaluation of agents should report accuracy jointly with tokens and turns, and that datasets of long documents should ship text and image renderings alongside each PDF.
