title: PixelOne: From Options to Pixels in a Single Forward for GUI Grounding
author: Kanghui Tian, Shuai Dong, Yuhan Zhu, Congcong Wang
contentSnippet:
Authors: Kanghui Tian , Shuai Dong , Yuhan Zhu , Congcong Wang , Ji Zhao , Tianxiang Jiang , Zhixiong Zhang , Shengyuan Ding , Yi Wang , Jiaqi Wang , Yu Qiao

Abstract: GUI grounding requires precise clicks at low latency. Recent models such as GUI-Decisions and GUI-Swift predict coordinates in one forward pass using fixed global bins with local refinement. However, screenshot downsampling removes detail needed to locate small controls, while fixed bins cover larger pixel ranges at higher resolutions. We introduce PixelOne, which transfers spatial knowledge from a search teacher to a student that predicts clicks directly from screenshots at native resolution. The teacher uses VideoJEV's text-option scorer to select rows and columns and progressively zoom into candidate regions. The student inherits the teacher's parameters and matches its distributions over explored regions through spatial distillation alongside box supervision. At inference, the same decision head selects a visual token, and a lightweight pixel head predicts the click within it, all in one forward pass. A click-aligned loss encourages pixels inside the target box to score above those outside. Across four benchmarks, PixelOne-Pro-35B-A3B achieves 83.8% mean accuracy, the highest among the evaluated single-forward grounders, with a mean latency of 0.43 s per target.

summary.tldr:
PixelOne is a GUI grounding model developed by researchers from Shanghai AI Lab and collaborators, designed to achieve high-precision click prediction in a single forward pass. Unlike existing models like GUI-Decisions and GUI-Swift that rely on fixed global bins and screenshot downsampling—which often obscures small UI elements—PixelOne utilizes a teacher-student distillation framework to maintain native resolution accuracy. The teacher model leverages VideoJEV’s text-option scorer to perform progressive zooming into candidate regions, while the student model learns to predict clicks directly from full-resolution screenshots by matching the teacher's spatial distributions and utilizing box supervision.

At inference, PixelOne employs a unified decision head to select a visual token, followed by a lightweight pixel head that predicts the specific click coordinate within that token. The architecture incorporates a click-aligned loss function to ensure pixels within target bounding boxes receive higher scores than those outside. The model, specifically the PixelOne-Pro-35B-A3B variant, achieves a mean accuracy of 83.8% across four benchmarks with a mean latency of 0.43 seconds per target, outperforming other single-forward grounding models.
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** PixelOne uses a teacher-student distillation approach where the student inherits spatial knowledge from a teacher that performs progressive zooming.
**Inference Efficiency:** The model operates in a single forward pass, utilizing a decision head for token selection and a lightweight pixel head for coordinate prediction.
**Performance Metrics:** The PixelOne-Pro-35B-A3B model achieves 83.8% mean accuracy across four benchmarks.
**Latency:** The system maintains a mean latency of 0.43 seconds per target.
**Technical Innovation:** The model addresses the resolution loss inherent in downsampling by predicting clicks directly from native resolution screenshots.

title: GlanceNav: Efficient Vision-and-Language Navigation with Streaming Memory and Counterfactual Rewind
author: Anh Dao, Quan-Dung Pham, Danh Vinh Le, Tuyen Pham Le
contentSnippet:
Authors: Anh Dao , Quan-Dung Pham , Danh Vinh Le , Tuyen Pham Le , Quan Nguyen , Yuzhang Shang

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become strong policies for vision-and-language navigation (VLN). However, most of them encode a sample of past frames again at every decision and are trained on isolated decisions, so computation is redundant and the usable history is short. They also learn from their own mistakes through outcome rewards that give one scalar to a whole episode. We ask whether a navigator can encode each frame only once, at a constant cost per step, and still remember what matters and learn efficiently from its mistakes. We present GlanceNav, a streaming navigator built on a hybrid MLLM. Its Gated DeltaNet layers carry a recurrent state through the whole episode, while its attention layers keep a short window of recent observations and a small bank of keyframes, selected by how much each frame changes the recurrent state. This constant-size memory keeps the cost per step fixed and allows training on whole episodes with the same memory as at inference. Because the entire memory can also be copied in constant time, we further propose Counterfactual Rewind (CoRe), a reinforcement learning stage that rewinds a drifting rollout to its closest approach to the goal, lets an expert correct a few actions, and credits decisions by the resulting change in outcome. Trained only on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE training splits, with 1,000 instructions for reinforcement learning, a 4B GlanceNav reaches success rates of 71.9% and 73.6% on R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen. On R2R-CE, it outperforms the strongest previous single-RGB method trained without external data by 9.1 points, while running at 104 ms per step.

summary.tldr:
GlanceNav is a vision-and-language navigation (VLN) model developed by Anh Dao, Quan-Dung Pham, Danh Vinh Le, Tuyen Pham Le, Quan Nguyen, and Yuzhang Shang. The 4B parameter model addresses the computational redundancy of traditional MLLMs, which typically re-encode past frames at every decision step. By utilizing a hybrid architecture that combines Gated DeltaNet layers for recurrent state management with an attention-based mechanism for short-term observation windows and keyframe storage, GlanceNav maintains a constant-size memory footprint and fixed computational cost per step.

The model introduces Counterfactual Rewind (CoRe), a reinforcement learning technique that identifies the point of maximum goal proximity during a drifting rollout, allows an expert to intervene, and assigns credit based on the resulting outcome change. Trained exclusively on R2R-CE and RxR-CE training splits using 1,000 instructions for reinforcement learning, the model achieves success rates of 71.9% on R2R-CE val-unseen and 73.6% on RxR-CE val-unseen. It outperforms the previous leading single-RGB method (trained without external data) by 9.1 percentage points on R2R-CE while maintaining an inference speed of 104 ms per step.
takeaways: **Architecture:** Uses Gated DeltaNet layers for recurrent state tracking combined with a selective keyframe bank to maintain constant-size memory.
**Performance:** Achieves 71.9% success rate on R2R-CE val-unseen and 73.6% on RxR-CE val-unseen.
**Efficiency:** Operates at a fixed cost of 104 ms per step, avoiding the redundant re-encoding of past frames.
**Training Methodology:** Employs Counterfactual Rewind (CoRe) to perform reinforcement learning by rewinding failed rollouts to the closest point of goal proximity for expert correction.
**Competitive Advantage:** Outperforms the strongest prior single-RGB method trained without external data by 9.1 points on the R2R-CE benchmark.

title: Frontier models need only one text to unmask its human or AI author
author: Atrey Desai, Deniz Bölöni-Turgut, Ty Brassington, Minjoon Choi
contentSnippet:
Authors: Atrey Desai , Deniz Bölöni-Turgut , Ty Brassington , Minjoon Choi , Jenna Russell , Rishanth Rajendhran , Bradley Emi , Hila Gonen , Hal Daumé III , John Wieting , Marzena Karpinska , Mohit Iyyer

Abstract: Given a single text and a simple zero-shot prompt (no web access, tools, candidate lists, or writing samples), frontier models can answer "who wrote this?" at three increasingly specific levels: (1) whether an AI or human wrote it, (2) if an AI, which lab, and (3) if a human, often exactly who. The latest models (Claude Fable 5.2, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Carbon) match trained detectors like Pangram while also explaining their predictions in natural language, and Opus 5.5 names the correct lab for 98% of texts generated by models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. Most strikingly, Fable 5.2 correctly names the author of 55% of 15K anonymous ICML 2020 reviews that were never made public, and identifies the username behind 69% of comments from active Redditors (with >500 posts over the last year). Accuracy depends on exposure to an author's writing in pretraining data and on reasoning effort, and simply asking a model how familiar it is with someone predicts whether it can identify their writing. For anyone who has published enough writing online, frontier models present a greater threat to anonymity than commonly assumed, and defenses are limited.

summary.tldr:
A research team including Atrey Desai, Mohit Iyyer, and Hal Daumé III demonstrates that frontier models can identify the authorship of text—distinguishing between human and AI, identifying specific AI labs, and pinpointing individual human authors—using only a single text sample and zero-shot prompting. The study highlights that models such as Claude Fable 5.2, GPT-6.1 Sol, and Gemini 4 Carbon achieve performance parity with specialized detectors like Pangram while providing natural language explanations for their reasoning. Notably, Opus 5.5 achieves a 98% accuracy rate in identifying the originating lab for texts generated by Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google models.

The research reveals significant privacy implications for online anonymity, with Fable 5.2 correctly identifying the authors of 55% of 15,000 private ICML 2020 reviews and 69% of comments from active Redditors with at least 500 posts. The authors establish that identification accuracy is directly correlated with the model's exposure to an author's writing during pretraining and the amount of reasoning effort applied. A simple self-assessment prompt asking the model about its familiarity with a specific author serves as a reliable predictor of its success in identifying that author's work, suggesting that existing defenses against such deanonymization are currently insufficient.
takeaways: **Model Performance:** Opus 5.5 achieves 98% accuracy in attributing text to specific AI labs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google).
**Anonymity Risks:** Fable 5.2 identified the authors of 55% of 15,000 non-public ICML 2020 reviews and 69% of active Reddit users with 500+ posts.
**Predictive Metric:** A model's self-reported familiarity with an author's writing style is a strong predictor of its ability to correctly identify that author.
**Methodology:** The identification process requires no web access, external tools, or reference writing samples, relying solely on zero-shot prompting.

title: Self-Supervised Dataset Distillation via Mutual Information Maximization
author: Mohammad Hossein Moslemi, Mahdi Beitollahi, Zhimin Mei, Jiale Cai
contentSnippet: Dataset distillation (DD) aims to compress a large dataset into a small synthetic one that remains effective for training neural networks. Despite its success in supervised learning, DD remains underexplored in self-supervised learning (SSL), where distilled data must preserve the information needed to learn representations that remain consistent across augmentations. To bridge this gap, we introduce Mutual Information Prototype Alignment (MIPA), an efficient SSL dataset distillation approach that optimizes synthetic images to preserve augmentation-invariant information. Specifically, MIPA treats synthetic images as learnable prototypes and uses a frozen encoder to assign real samples to them based on feature similarity. A synthetic dataset that preserves such augmentation invariance should yield stable prototype assignments across multiple augmented views of the same real image. MIPA encourages this by maximizing mutual information between cross-view assignments while avoiding trivial solutions in which all real samples are assigned to only a few synthetic prototypes. Evaluations on image classification benchmarks show that synthetic data generated by MIPA yield higher-quality representations than existing distillation approaches while reducing time and storage demands during distillation.

title: CCFinance: Reconstructing Financial News Samples from Web Archives
author: Marcus Gawronsky
contentSnippet: Proprietary news archives assign stories to firms, so reproducing a financial study often requires access to both the articles and the vendor's assignments. CCFinance lets researchers reconstruct firm coverage under different selection rules by recording which version of a story was captured, which issuers it names and how often each appears. From 14.8 million English-language records in Fine News, derived from public Common Crawl News, we identify 5.22 million distinct, consistently dated articles with issuer links. Exact reconstruction requires the restricted snapshot and derived artifacts. We compare GLiNER and Stanza on 250 model-labeled article leads and assess issuer links and story focus against blinded model judgments. Estimated precision among 475 accepted links is 96.8%. Among held-out articles with a detected company, requiring three mentions raises subject precision from 31.9% to 66.1%. Across the 2017-2025 panel, the same rule reduces the number of issuer-years with at least 50 qualifying stories from 13,918 to 8,641. Three reimplementations examine volatility tracking, bank networks and overnight returns. In the network study, bank pairs appearing together rose from 177 to 242 across publishers between January and April 2020, but fell from 50 to 35 within Reuters.

title: Unlocking the Power of Loops in Pretrained LLMs with Loop Residuals
author: Xuanlei Zhao, Hailun Xu, Kai Wang, Yang Luo
contentSnippet: Looped Transformers iterate a shared block of layers to increase computation without adding parameters, offering stronger performance and test-time scaling. However, this power has so far required training from scratch and yielded only modest gains for LLMs. Finetuning existing models into loops is far cheaper, yet also brings only marginal gains over SFT. We propose LoopRes, an effective, scalable, and simple approach that turns loops into significant and consistent gains for pretrained LLMs. Building on Attention Residuals, LoopRes lets each looped layer attend directly to the outputs of earlier loops. Since these outputs are iterates of the same layers and become harder to tell apart, we give each a trainable loop-aware key that encodes its structural identity. Attending to all earlier loops also lets layers skip intermediate ones, so we restrict each layer to a residual window of the latest W loops, forcing every loop to build incrementally on recent ones. Across 6 pretrained LLMs from 3 model families and 9 benchmarks, LoopRes delivers significant and consistent gains: at 2x compute, it improves Qwen3-1.7B-Base by 29.1% over SFT, more than doubling the gain of the state-of-the-art baseline. The gains hold on larger models up to 30B and across all three families. More importantly, from 1.7B to 8B, LoopRes scales more steeply than SFT as compute grows, reaching a higher ceiling while needing less compute on long outputs. These results establish LoopRes as an effective looping approach, delivering both better performance and better test-time scaling.

title: Lyris: Layout-Guided Long Video Generation with Persistent 3D Memory
author: Chen Wang, Jiahui Huang, Riccardo de Lutio, Alex Trevithick
contentSnippet: Exploring a scene from as little as a single photo requires generating a long, camera-controlled walkthrough that extends far beyond what was captured, yet remains consistent upon return. Memory-based video generation methods preserve what they have already seen, but have no anchor beyond it, where the camera drifts from its path and a text prompt can name objects but not place them. Layout-conditioned methods provide such an anchor and precise control over what appears where, but rely on layouts that are typically authored by hand. Both limitations arise because, beyond what was captured, nothing anchors the video model unless a human authors one. To overcome both, we propose Lyris, a long video generation framework that never leaves the video model without an anchor: a persistent point-cloud memory where the scene has been observed or generated, and a 3D layout that a vision-language model authors where it has not. Our key insight is that the interface between the two models can be surprisingly coarse. A layout of one labeled 3D box per object is simple enough for a vision-language model to author (and for a user to edit), yet expressive enough for a video model to follow once rendered along the camera path. We demonstrate walkthroughs of over three minutes and 50 meters from a single photo, passing through doorways into rooms it never shows. When evaluated on minute-long round trips across four datasets, Lyris outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a wide margin, reducing camera error by 3.8x and improving consistency upon return by 22% on average.

title: Innata-0: A Native Embodied World System with Model-Agent Co-Design
author: Innata Team, Yu Bai, Ziyi Bai, Yuxuan Cai
contentSnippet: The physical world is open-ended, dynamic, and partially observable. While foundation models have advanced embodied intelligence, standalone models struggle with long-horizon execution, and simply integrating models with agents may lead to inconsistencies between planning and physical control. To support reliable and adaptive behaviors in the physical world, we introduce Innata-0, a native embodied world system. Innata-0 jointly designs an embodied world-action model and an agent to combine their complementary strengths. The model, Innata-0-WAM, adopts a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that integrates understanding, prediction, and action generation. The agent, Innata-0-Agent, coordinates long-horizon execution through memory, verification, and recovery. A co-design protocol is further proposed to align model training with agent execution and leverage validated experiences to support subsequent adaptation and model improvement. Extensive evaluations demonstrate strong embodied capabilities across understanding, world prediction, and robotic manipulation. Innata-0 represents our first step toward physical intelligence, and we see it as the beginning of a much longer journey.

Innata-0 jointly designs an embodied world-action model and an agent to combine their complementary strengths. The model, Innata-0-WAM, adopts a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that integrates understanding, prediction, and action generation. The agent, Innata-0-Agent, coordinates long-horizon execution through memory, verification, and recovery.
takeaways: A co-design protocol is further proposed to align model training with agent execution and leverage validated experiences to support subsequent adaptation and model improvement.
Extensive evaluations demonstrate strong embodied capabilities across understanding, world prediction, and robotic manipulation.

title: WorldLatent: A Unified 4D Latent Space for World Perception and Generation
author: Jingxi Chen, Yujia Chen, Cornelia Fermuller, Yiannis Aloimonos
contentSnippet: Generative Pre-Training (GPT) represents a profound milestone in natural language processing, serving as the foundation for most of today's state-of-the-art large language models. By casting diverse understanding and generation problems into a shared token representation, GPT enables a single architecture and unified optimization loop to master heterogeneous tasks across massive corpora, giving rise to powerful foundation models for natural language. In contrast, 4D spatiotemporal vision lacks a common representational protocol: perception (such as depth and camera estimation) and generation are either handled by separate one-way pipelines or bolted together from unaligned single-modality spaces. In this work, we introduce WorldLatent, a framework that formulates a unified 4D latent space as a common protocol for both world perception and generation. Rather than relying on fragmented, task-specific models or stacked single-modality representations, our framework proposes a multimodal VAE architecture that compresses and fuses complex 4D visual appearance, geometry, and dynamics into a single structured latent representation. Within this formulation, perception and generation operate as complementary denoising processes over the same latent space, enabling one generative model to learn both capabilities simultaneously within a single training loop. Experiments across representative 4D benchmarks verify that our fused latent protocol achieves specialist-level zero-shot 4D perception, coherent 4D generation, and controllable editing from a single model. By demonstrating that diverse 4D tasks can be seamlessly unified under a shared representational protocol, our work provides a scalable foundation for general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence.

title: AdProducer: Towards Agentic Advertising Video Generation
author: Kunyang Li, Chaoyang Wang, Mubarak Shah, Yuzhang Shang
contentSnippet: Recent advances in video generation have made automated advertising production increasingly feasible. However, an effective advertisement must faithfully represent the product and communicate its selling points through compelling visual storytelling, which requires more than visual synthesis: it calls for deeper product understanding and strategic decisions about how to present product value. Crucially, product research and creative design are closely intertwined, as the information gathered about a product determines which features can be faithfully demonstrated and how they should be presented. In this paper, we introduce AdProducer, the first end-to-end agentic framework for advertising video creation, transforming concise creative briefs into finished advertisements. Our multimodal agent autonomously researches products through web and image search and translates its findings into selling-point-driven storyboards that guide a frozen video generator. To achieve this, we develop a dedicated data construction pipeline that yields two training datasets, AdProducer-SFT and AdProducer-RL, and train the agent through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning with joint optimization of storyboard- and video-level rewards. We further introduce AdCreation-Bench, comprising 305 advertising briefs across eight domains, with two complementary metrics: PG-Score for product correctness and creative execution, and Ad-Score for overall advertising effectiveness assessed by an independent judge. Experiments demonstrate that AdProducer improves the PG-Score of MiniMax H3 from 17.3 to 51.3 and generalizes to Veo 3.1 without additional training, improving its score from 28.0 to 35.9, with consistent gains in Ad-Score, VideoScore2, and human evaluations. Code, models, and data are released.

title: Do learned image captioning metrics generalize? Auditing duplicated samples in human-judgment benchmarks
author: Xiaochen Zhang, Jin Li, Chunlong Xia, Longjiang Guo
contentSnippet: Learned image captioning metrics are trained and tested on human judgments, so their reported correlation is a claim about generalization. We audit this claim for the three most recent collections of such judgments, Polaris, Nebula, and Spica, matching images at the pixel level. First, test samples reappear in training sets: the Spica training set contains about two-thirds of the Polaris test set, with identical human ratings. Second, controlled retraining shows that duplicates can inflate a metric: for Pearl, the gain is confined to the duplicated samples and grows with every epoch; for DENEB, it stays below one point. The gain depends on the learner and on how often a training set repeats a sample. Third, Kendall's τ over all samples is the sum of two terms, detecting captions with the lowest human score and ranking the others; the first supplies most of the reported correlation and is nearly saturated. The recent test sets cannot order Polos, DENEB and Pearl consistently, and a ridge regression on frozen features matches or exceeds all three. Fourth, we propose a protocol that ranks a learned metric only with a model trained without test samples, reports both terms, and compares metrics by paired tests. Under it, zero-shot vision--language judges rank first on the three recent test sets, and a fine-tuned judge ranks first on the three earlier benchmarks. The same analysis applies to any evaluator learned from human judgments; filter lists and code are released at https://github.com/morninghut/ic-dataset-audit .

title: OWE-Bench: A long-horizon benchmark for measuring real-world engineering
author: Jacob Cole, Martin Dimakis, Victor Barres, Bertie Vidgen
contentSnippet:
Authors: Jacob Cole , Martin Dimakis , Victor Barres , Bertie Vidgen , Edward Hu , Jason Wei

Abstract: We present OWE-Bench (OpenWorldEngineer-Bench), a benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering tasks written by domain experts in software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and scientific computing. Tasks range from optimizing kernels and designing an aircraft, to identifying the faults responsible for an earthquake. Each task requires significant domain knowledge and engineering work, with models averaging hundreds of millions of tokens per task. Solutions are scored on practical measures such as speed, cost and accuracy, both on provided cases the agent could test against and on hidden cases that an engineer would expect from the task description. The best-performing frontier model so far, Claude Fable 5.2, scores 54.6% and averages 211 million tokens per task. We highlight two findings. First, when models are given more time, they use more test-time compute and achieve higher scores. Models also scale differently with test-time compute: GPT-6 Astra achieves higher scores at shorter time limits and at equal token use, while Claude Fable 5.2 uses more tokens at longer limits to achieve the highest overall score. Second, each model scores lower on hidden cases than on the provided cases, by an average of 18 points, which we call the deployment gap. Models also fail to predict the deployment gap, overestimating their performance on hidden test cases by an average of 21 points. We hope that OWE-Bench grounds progress toward agents whose engineering solutions perform as well in deployment as they do in testing.

title: Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation: Pixel as Code for Agentic Visual Creation
author: Guo Chen, Fuxiao Liu, Haoqin Tu, Yiyang Zhou
contentSnippet: Visual creation demands expressive imagery together with precise control over text, layout, and structure. We introduce Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation, an agentic framework that connects these capabilities through Pixel as Code. Raster images are represented by learned discrete visual tokens, while structured artifacts use explicit programs. A shared generation-and-rendering interface connects these representations to visual feedback across images, vector graphics, webpages, and documents. A Nemotron-native harness coordinates planning and raster candidate selection, with targeted repair for editable structured and hybrid artifacts. To support this interface, we develop Nemotron-Labs-Image-Tokenizer, the autoregressive raster generator Nemotron-Labs-Image-30B-A3B, and the structured-code model family Nemotron-Labs-VisionCode. On approximately 178K images spanning six visual domains, our tokenizer improves reconstruction PSNR from 26.08 to 29.57 dB over Emu3.5 IBQ. It also provides 7.13x faster encoding and 10.93x faster decoding at batch size one on A100. In standalone evaluation, one Nemotron-Labs-VisionCode variant surpasses Kimi K3.1 Pro on the aggregate across Chart2Code, MMSVG, Design2Code, and Image2Struct. At the system level, the Nemotron-native configuration raises GenEval2 Soft-TIFA GM from 31.71 to 52.56 using the same raster generator. With our best setting, Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation achieves performance competitive with GPT Image 2 and Nano Banana Pro across most benchmarks with available comparisons.

title: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment
author: Peter Horvath, Ilia Shumailov, Zhuoran Liu, Lukasz Chmielewski
contentSnippet: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces without crashing the system while preserving model coherence. Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor running Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, localized physical faults reliably force models to fulfill restricted requests, demonstrating that model-level alignment provides no robust security guarantees without hardware-level fault tolerance. Finally, we demonstrate the physical-world consequences of this vulnerability on an active 6-DoF robotic manipulator controlled by a SmolVLA vision-language-action policy. Our attack silently corrupts the model forcing the arm into abrupt, hazardous lunges; in two instances the robotic arm attempted to pinch the paper author -- proving that hardware faults can directly translate into real physical harm.

title: Foresight Forcing: Learning Spatial Foresight for Robotic Manipulation
author: Mishuo Han, Zhixuan Liang, Zhaoyuan Wan, Wendi Chen
contentSnippet: Robotic manipulation policies can improve action prediction by anticipating how objects move and how their spatial relationships change. World Action Models (WAMs) learn to predict future visual observations, but their training objectives typically leave the underlying 3D geometric transitions implicit. To alleviate this problem, we introduce Foresight Forcing (F^{2}), a WAM that learns a spatial transition representation from changes in a pretrained 3D feature space. During training, a frozen 3D foundation model extracts patch-wise feature differences from aligned current and future observations that provide dense supervision for geometry-aware feature transitions. We distill these targets into spatial transition queries, which are progressively refined from the current observation, language instruction, and proprioceptive state, and use them alongside current visual features to generate actions. At deployment, the policy predicts the queries without future observations or the 3D teacher. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin2.0 demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved robustness, including 95.01% average success on RoboTwin2.0 Full. On six real-world manipulation tasks, F^{2} achieves a mean task score of 85.8%.

title: We haven’t seen the last of the major tech outages
author: Terrence O’Brien
contentSnippet: Over the last week or so, we have seen a nationwide FAA ground stop, a multi-day Outlook outage that brought entire companies to a standstill, and a banking outage at JPMorgan Chase. But the consensus is that there are more to come. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN: > “The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.” Microsoft President Brad Smith issued a similar warning about further outages to CBS, but sounded a much more ominous tone. > “I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn’t the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks … The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now.” While the outages over the last week were believed to be caused by cyberattacks, Smith said that AI has made it easier to find flaws, “and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you’re a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems,” he said. The last few months have also seen an increase in attacks on government and commercial systems, including those at the USDA, JP Morgan, and supermarkets. Whether outages are brought on by AI-assisted hackers or human error during the rush to patch an aging system, one thing seems certain: there will be more in the coming months.

summary.tldr:
Recent critical infrastructure failures, including a nationwide FAA ground stop, a multi-day Microsoft Outlook outage, and a JPMorgan Chase banking disruption, signal a period of heightened instability in global information systems. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Microsoft President Brad Smith have both publicly warned that these incidents are likely to persist as the global information infrastructure undergoes a massive, systemic upgrade. Clayton emphasized that rapid shifts in compute and application technology inherently introduce operational volatility, necessitating significant long-term investment in cybersecurity and system modernization.

Microsoft President Brad Smith characterized the current environment as a precarious transition period, noting that the global infrastructure upgrade will not be completed in a short timeframe. Smith highlighted the dual-use nature of AI in this context: while AI tools assist in identifying and patching code vulnerabilities, they simultaneously lower the barrier for malicious actors to exploit those same flaws. This technological arms race, combined with the pressure to patch aging legacy systems, has contributed to a recent surge in cyberattacks targeting government agencies like the USDA and commercial entities, suggesting that further outages are an expected byproduct of the current digital transformation cycle.
takeaways: **Recent Incidents:** Major outages have recently impacted the FAA, Microsoft Outlook, and JPMorgan Chase, alongside reported attacks on the USDA and various supermarket chains.
**AI Dual-Use:** AI is accelerating both the discovery of software vulnerabilities for defensive patching and the exploitation of those same flaws by malicious actors.
**Systemic Upgrades:** Microsoft President Brad Smith stated that the global information infrastructure is currently undergoing a comprehensive upgrade that will take months, not weeks, to stabilize.
**Official Outlook:** Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton explicitly linked the current "bumps in the road" to the rapid step-change in compute and application technology.

title: OpenAI’s chief scientist has thoughts on how to limit AI development
author: Anthony Ha
contentSnippet:
A new blog post from OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki discusses potential limits on AI development, with a focus on a measurement called perplexity.

Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher said the companies were “gambling with our lives,” and even Anthropic’s IPO filing suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then published a plan to “pace the frontier,” seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Among other things, Amodei called for companies to agree to “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.”

But to establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how you measure speed. Pachocki’s post — described by Altman as “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while” — suggests perplexity (not to be confused with the company of the same name ) could be that measurement.

In Pachochki’s argument, benchmarks that focus on AI’s “downstream capabilities” have quickly become outdated as the technology advances. But perplexity — which “measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions” — has remained “informative.”

Pachochki’s post includes a chart of how the perplexity of OpenAI’s models has fallen since GPT 3.5.

“GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models,” he wrote. “Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.”

So in his view, perplexity could provide the basis for “a shared benchmark for general intelligence,” which AI companies could then use to establish “common limits.” With perplexity serving as a standard measurement for AI progress, the companies would commit not to go past a certain threshold “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone.”

summary.tldr:
OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki has proposed using model perplexity as a standardized metric to regulate the pace of AI development. In a post endorsed by CEO Sam Altman as a critical publication, Pachocki argues that while downstream capability benchmarks quickly become obsolete, perplexity—the average measure of a model's ability to predict the next token—remains a consistent and informative indicator of progress.

Pachocki’s analysis highlights a correlation between declining perplexity scores and the emergence of advanced reasoning capabilities. Specifically, he notes that GPT-4 achieved a perplexity of approximately 0.91, which enabled effective chain-of-thought reasoning, while models reaching losses below 0.8 have demonstrated transformative capabilities in domains such as mathematics and cybersecurity. The proposal suggests that AI companies could adopt these perplexity thresholds as a shared benchmark to establish voluntary speed limits, pausing development until safety and monitoring milestones are met.
takeaways: **Core Metric:** Perplexity is defined as the average ability of a model to predict the next token, where lower values indicate higher predictive accuracy.
**Historical Benchmarks:** OpenAI’s GPT-4 model recorded a perplexity score of approximately 0.91.
**Capability Threshold:** Models achieving perplexity scores below 0.8 have shown the emergence of transformative capabilities in cybersecurity and mathematics.

**Regulatory Proposal:** The framework suggests using specific perplexity levels as a 'shared benchmark' to trigger mandatory pauses in development until monitoring capabilities reach defined milestones.

title: NVIDIA Releases Alpamayo 2 Edge: A 2B Reasoning VLA for DRIVE Thor
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: NVIDIA has released Alpamayo 2 Edge , a compact reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) model for autonomous driving. Alpamayo 2 Edge is a 2B-parameter model that plans trajectories and explains them inside the vehicle. It targets NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor , not a datacenter GPU. The goal: reasoning-based planning within onboard compute and latency budgets. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 2B-class. Card breakdown: 2.45B backbone + 0.2B action expert (HF metadata says 3B). Context length: not disclosed (measured prompt: 3,236 tokens). Runs on: NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor with the FP8 + TensorRT Edge-LLM recipe. BF16 PyTorch needs 16 GB+ GPU memory, validated on 1x H100 80GB. Performance: Strong closed-loop driver for its size; mid-pack on reasoning QA. Best: 15.15 km per at-fault incident in AlpaSim, about 60x Qwen-Drive-1.0 4B (0.25 km). Worst: nuReasoning numeric score of 48.67; LingoQA 75.2 trails Alpamayo 2 Super (79.2). Bottom line: Best: reasoning-based planning at 160 to 190 ms on in-car hardware. Worst: only H100 validated, and real-time Thor speed needs the FP8 recipe. What is Alpamayo 2 Edge? Alpamayo 2 Edge is an open NVIDIA VLA model that turns surround-camera video into a 6.4-second plan. It is the in-car member of the Alpamayo family , next to the 34B cloud model Alpamayo 2 Super . Per the model card , the 2.45B backbone pairs a 1.96B language model with a 0.41B SigLIP2 encoder. A 0.2B diffusion action expert sits on top. The backbone comes from NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Edge and is Nemotron-based. NVIDIA markets the model as 2B, while Hugging Face metadata shows 3B. What goes in and what comes out? For trajectory prediction, the model reads 6 cameras and 22 frames per observation. The 2 front cameras give 5 frames each, the other 4 give 3 each. It also takes a navigation instruction and 20 historical ego poses. Output is 64 waypoints from 0.1 to 6.4 seconds. The action expert predicts acceleration and curvature, then a unicycle model integrates them. The text output is a Chain-of-Causation (CoC) reasoning trace. The model also answers free-form questions about a driving scene. How does adaptive reasoning work? During routine driving, the model emits special <NOMINAL> tokens instead of a full reasoning trace. summary.tldr:
NVIDIA has released Alpamayo 2 Edge, a 2B-parameter vision-language-action (VLA) model specifically engineered for the NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor platform. Designed for onboard autonomous driving, the model performs trajectory planning and scene explanation within strict latency constraints. It functions as the edge-deployed counterpart to the 34B-parameter Alpamayo 2 Super cloud model, utilizing a backbone derived from NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Edge and Nemotron architecture. The model is designed to process surround-camera video to generate a 6.4-second trajectory plan, outputting 64 waypoints alongside a Chain-of-Causation (CoC) reasoning trace.

Technically, the model architecture consists of a 2.45B backbone—comprising a 1.96B language model and a 0.41B SigLIP2 encoder—paired with a 0.2B diffusion-based action expert. Input data includes 6 camera feeds (22 frames total), navigation instructions, and 20 historical ego poses. For real-time in-car performance, the model requires an FP8 + TensorRT Edge-LLM recipe to achieve inference speeds of 160 to 190 ms on DRIVE AGX Thor hardware. While BF16 PyTorch execution has been validated on a single H100 80GB GPU, it requires over 16 GB of VRAM. The model employs adaptive reasoning, emitting special tokens during routine driving and reserving full CoC traces for complex scenarios to minimize token count and latency.

In performance benchmarks, Alpamayo 2 Edge achieved 15.15 km per at-fault incident in the AlpaSim environment, significantly outperforming Qwen-Drive-1.0 4B (0.25 km). However, it trails the larger Alpamayo 2 Super in LingoQA scores (75.2 vs 79.2) and recorded a nuReasoning numeric score of 48.67. While marketed as a 2B model, Hugging Face metadata indicates a 3B parameter count. The model is currently limited by its reliance on H100 validation for development, with real-time deployment contingent on the specific FP8 optimization recipe.
takeaways: **Architecture Composition:** 2.45B backbone (1.96B language model + 0.41B SigLIP2 encoder) plus a 0.2B diffusion action expert.
**Input/Output Specs:** Processes 6 cameras (22 frames), navigation instructions, and 20 ego poses to output 64 waypoints (0.1 to 6.4 seconds).
**Performance Metrics:** Achieved 15.15 km per at-fault incident in AlpaSim and a 75.2 score on LingoQA.
**Latency Targets:** Operates at 160 to 190 ms on DRIVE AGX Thor hardware using the FP8 + TensorRT Edge-LLM recipe.
**Adaptive Reasoning:** Emits special tokens for routine driving and full Chain-of-Causation traces only for complex scenes to reduce compute load.

title: Position-Skipped Distillation of Sparse-Attention Indexers: Train Short, Serve Long
author: Fu Dai
contentSnippet: Top-k sparse attention relies on an indexer, a lightweight per-layer module that ranks cached tokens so attention covers only the k highest-scoring ones. Indexers are usually distilled from dense attention at the full serving length, so every training step pays for long-context dense attention. We show that when an indexer is distilled on short sequences, its failure to generalise to longer contexts is driven mainly by rotary positional encoding (RoPE), not by degraded content matching. We propose position-skipped distillation: the indexer and the frozen teacher see short sequences whose position IDs contain a randomly placed gap, so neither ever processes more than the short training length. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B, an indexer distilled on 8K tokens this way matches a 32K-distilled indexer to within about 0.5 perplexity up to 32K, and on DeepSeek-V2-Lite matches a 64K-distilled indexer at 64K with roughly 6x less training compute per token. On Llama-3.1-8B it trails the stronger 32K run by 0.6 perplexity, and at 64K simple position compression is often as good, so the main gain is training cost rather than quality. We also quantise indexer keys to 3-4 bits without retraining and score them with a fused integer kernel: at 4 bits, perplexity changes by at most 0.05 and the scan is 1.6-2.2x faster than half precision. In a current serving engine, the indexer speeds up decoding only for long contexts with multiple concurrent streams.

title: Why data centers are at the center of the Big Tech backlash
author: Anthony Ha
contentSnippet:
In his new book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine.

The book is well-timed, to put it mildly, as data center backlash seems to have been one of the motivators for the massive blue wave seen in the recent midterm elections . And those debates are likely to continue as Democrats wield more governmental power .

In an interview with TechCrunch, Marx described the data center buildout as “fundamentally unsustainable” and “completely out of line with a livable planet,” while also arguing that these facilities make for an obvious target amidst broader anger at the tech industry. After all, if a data center is being built in your community, “it’s very physical, it’s very material.”

“It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on,“ Marx said. “You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.”

He also suggested that data center opposition is only the most visible piece of a wider movement targeting “the physical manifestations of the tech industry, […] whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.”

During our conversation (which I’ve edited for length and clarity), Marx and I discussed data centers’ environmental impact, how tech companies are responding to community resistance, and what it’s actually like inside a data center.

Getting inside of a hyperscale data center was not the easiest task in the world. I spoke to some researchers who have been doing research on data centers for a number of years longer than I had, and they told me that before the generative AI moment, and before all the a

summary.tldr:
In his book 'Hyperscale,' journalist Paris Marx examines the environmental and social impact of the global data center buildout, framing the infrastructure as a 'fundamentally unsustainable' manifestation of Big Tech’s expansionist ambitions. Marx argues that the physical presence of these facilities—which consume vast quantities of electricity and water—has turned them into political flashpoints, citing community resistance in regions like Chile, Ireland, and Oregon as evidence of a growing backlash against the tech industry's resource demands.

Technically, Marx describes the modern hyperscale data center as a highly securitized, utilitarian environment characterized by extreme noise levels from cooling fans and strict access controls requiring passport verification and key-card authentication for every internal door. The book highlights specific instances of resource strain, such as data centers consuming over 20% of Ireland’s electricity, leading to a 2022 grid connection moratorium in Dublin, and Google’s usage of 29% of the water supply in The Dalles, Oregon. Marx contends that the current trajectory of AI-driven infrastructure expansion is disconnected from tangible societal benefits, prioritizing corporate power over local community stability and environmental sustainability.
takeaways: **Ireland Grid Impact:** Data centers in Ireland consume over 20% of the country's total electricity, prompting a 2022 moratorium on new grid connections in the Dublin area.
**Oregon Water Usage:** Google’s data center operations in The Dalles, Oregon, were revealed to account for 29% of the city's total water consumption.

**Security Protocols:** Access to modern hyperscale facilities requires advance passport submission and multi-layered physical security, including key-card access for every individual door within the facility.

**Operational Environment:** Server rooms are described as utilitarian, high-temperature environments with extreme noise levels generated by cooling fans, necessitating hearing protection for extended stays.

**Community Resistance:** Opposition to data centers is categorized by Marx as part of a broader movement against the physical manifestations of Big Tech, including Flock cameras, Meta smart glasses, and Waymo autonomous vehicles.

title: Binding of Isaac developer removes AI music from Repentance Plus
author: Terrence O’Brien
contentSnippet: The Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus has spent the last few days getting review-bombed on Steam after it was discovered that a particular segment of the game used AI music. Reddit user ShweetsStuff discovered the songs used during a Grand Theft Auto-themed section. They found several audio files with Suno metadata that pointed back to the tracks on Suno’s site. Creator Edmund McMillen took to X to apologize and claimed he “had no idea” the in-game GTA parody used generative AI music. Adding to the drama, Valve requires developers to disclose how and when they use generative AI in the development process, and Nicalis, Inc., the studio behind Repentance Plus, doesn’t appear to have mentioned the AI music anywhere. [Media: https://twitter.com/edmundmcmillen/status/2124169167880470745?s=20] Within hours of the discovery, Nicalis shared on X that Repentance Plus had been updated and the generated music files had been removed. While reviews on Steam have yet to rebound, and the game is still rated as “overwhelmingly negative,” users on X seem to be giving McMillen the benefit of the doubt, likely because he’s been quite outspoken on AI in game development, calling it “uninspired and bland” in a TikTok from 2024. [Media: https://twitter.com/nicalis/status/2124241453266169887]

summary.tldr:
The Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus faced significant community backlash and Steam review-bombing following the discovery of AI-generated music within a Grand Theft Auto-themed segment of the game. Reddit user ShweetsStuff identified the tracks by locating Suno metadata embedded in the audio files, which linked directly to the Suno platform. This discovery triggered immediate scrutiny regarding compliance with Valve’s mandatory disclosure policies for generative AI usage in software development, which the publisher, Nicalis, Inc., reportedly failed to satisfy.

Creator Edmund McMillen publicly apologized on X, stating he was unaware that generative AI had been utilized in the game's development. McMillen has previously expressed public disdain for AI in game design, characterizing it as "uninspired and bland" in a 2024 TikTok. In response to the controversy, Nicalis, Inc. issued an update to remove the AI-generated audio files within hours of the initial discovery. Despite the removal, the game’s Steam rating remains "overwhelmingly negative" as of the latest reports.
takeaways: **Discovery Method:** Reddit user ShweetsStuff identified the AI music by finding Suno metadata embedded within the game's audio files.
**Regulatory Compliance:** The publisher, Nicalis, Inc., failed to disclose the use of generative AI to Valve, violating Steam's mandatory disclosure requirements for AI-integrated software.
**Remediation:** Nicalis, Inc. released an update to remove the AI-generated tracks within hours of the public discovery.
**Creator Stance:** Edmund McMillen, the game's creator, publicly disavowed the use of AI, citing his previously stated belief that such tools produce "uninspired and bland" content.

title: The vibe-coding revolution is coming to all the gadgets
author: David Pierce
contentSnippet: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the vibe-hacking of everything, follow David Pierce. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. How it started Like so many things with AI, it’s not that large language models opened up some wholly new capability. For as long as there have been gadgets, a few users have been hacking, modding, jailbreaking, and tweaking them to their liking. What is new is that it’s easy now. People all over the world are discovering that they can use large language models to hack their hardware simply by prompting Claude Code or Codex to do it. It has led to a boom in developer-friendly gadgets and created a market for better software on just about every device you can think of. For one developer in India who goes by Gathin T, the whole thing started almost on a whim. “One afternoon, I was fiddling with my TV, and it was just really shitty,” he tells me. His was a set made by Xiaomi and running Android TV, with so many ads and so much interface chaos it was hard to even change inputs. And he got to thinking: If you can install another launcher on your Android phone, maybe you can do the same to your TV. “The first thing that came to mind was to remove the bloatware from the TV,” he says. “Then I thought, why not make it look better?” Gathin prompted Claude Code and discovered that with a couple of permissions tweaks and a toggle of USB debugging mode, his chatbot could control his TV as long as they were on the same Wi-Fi network. An hour and a half later, Gathin had redesigned his TV to his liking — no more onscreen ads, a simpler interface, easier access to his PlayStation on another input. He posted on X about what he’d done and promptly went viral. So Gathin put together his work, bought a domain, and launched CleanYourTV as a tool for helping other people solve their own television interfaces. It became one of the most popular repositories on GitHub, got thousands of pull requests and feature ideas, and inspired countless people to point their own chatbot at their big screen. Gathin is careful to note that the only TVs that work this easily are based on Android. (He has Claude Code-d his way through other operating systems, but those involve more explicit jailbreaking and rooting, so he’s more reluctant to

summary.tldr:
The rise of 'vibe-coding'—using LLMs like Claude Code and Codex to reverse-engineer, modify, and jailbreak consumer hardware—is transforming the landscape of device customization. Developers and non-technical users are increasingly leveraging AI to bypass bloatware, unlock hidden APIs, and repackage firmware for devices ranging from Android-based TVs and cameras to synthesizers and gaming consoles. A notable example is the 'CleanYourTV' project, which allows users to strip ads and simplify interfaces on Xiaomi Android TVs by automating USB debugging and permission tweaks via LLM-generated scripts.

This trend has triggered a defensive response from manufacturers, particularly in the gaming sector, where companies are moving toward more invasive DRM and cloud-streaming architectures to prevent decompilation. Industry experts like former Take-Two AI head Luke Dicken suggest this will lead to a broader industry shift toward platform-level lockdowns. Conversely, some manufacturers are embracing the trend; for instance, M-Vave released open-source firmware for its FM-1 synthesizer to accommodate the hacker community. Meanwhile, the hardware ecosystem is shifting toward modular, developer-friendly platforms like ESP32 modules (e.g., M5Stack PaperMono), which are increasingly being used to build bespoke, single-purpose consumer devices, a movement Meta is currently supporting through its Muse Gadgets program.
takeaways: **CleanYourTV Methodology:** Uses LLMs to automate the removal of bloatware and interface customization on Android-based TVs by toggling USB debugging and modifying system permissions.
**Gaming Industry Response:** Executives anticipate a shift toward more invasive DRM and streaming-only models to mitigate the risks of AI-assisted decompilation and unauthorized platform porting.
**Hardware Shift:** The community is increasingly favoring ESP32-based modules over traditional jailbreaking, as these platforms are designed for custom firmware and modular functionality.
**Corporate Adoption:** Meta is actively entering the space with its 'Muse Gadgets' program, providing a pathway for users to deploy custom AI-driven software on ESP32 hardware.

**Risk Profile:** Vibe-coding carries significant bricking risks, leading developers like Gathin T to implement automated backup and verification agents within their tools to mitigate potential system failures.

title: Best Personal AI Agents in 2026: OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Gemini Spark and More, Compared on Memory, Security and Cost
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: A personal AI agent runs continuously, keeps memory across sessions, and acts inside your apps. You talk to it in a chat app, by email or by voice. It keeps working after you close the window. The category started small. OpenClaw began in November 2025 as Clawdbot, a weekend project by Peter Steinberger. Twelve months later, Google, OpenAI, Meta and Perplexity all ship their own versions. The products split into 2 camps. Self-hosted agents run on your machine or server and use any model you choose. Managed agents run on a vendor’s cloud VM and come bundled with a subscription. How we ranked them We scored each agent on 3 axes that matter once an agent holds your inbox and credentials. Memory: what persists, where it is stored, and whether you can read, edit or delete it. Security: default permissions, the isolation boundary, approval gates, and the public incident record. Cost: the subscription price, or token spend plus hosting for self-hosted options. Facts come from vendor documentation, launch posts and independent security research. Prices are US list prices as of November 21, 2026. Ranking reflects overall fit for an individual user, not raw capability. Comparison table Rank Agent Maker Runs on Memory Security default Starting cost Best for 1 Hermes Agent Nous Research Your machine or server; Docker, Modal, Daytona backends MEMORY.md, USER.md, SQLite FTS5 session search, self-written skills Manual approvals, denied on timeout; hardline denylist Free (MIT) + model tokens Developers who want an agent that learns 2 OpenClaw OpenClaw Foundation Your machine or server; opt-in sandbox Editable Markdown workspace files; SQLite sessions since 2.0 Full host access unless sandbox is enabled Free (MIT) + tokens; managed hosts ~$12–$49/mo Widest chat-channel reach 3 Gemini Spark Google Dedicated Google Cloud VMs Google account context via connected apps Asks before spending money or sending email $19.99/mo AI Pro (US) Google Workspace users 4 OpenAI dots OpenAI OpenAI cloud computer; optional connected computer Chats, ChatGPT memory and the dot’s own notes Proactive research is read-only; passwords hidden from model Included in eligible ChatGPT Pro and Business Premium plans ChatGPT and Codex power users 5 Meta Muse Meta Muse Secure VM in Meta’s cloud Learns preferences; forgets on request Sentinel agent gates internet access; approvals for email and purchases Fre

summary.tldr:
As of November 2026, the personal AI agent market has bifurcated into self-hosted solutions and managed cloud-based services. Leading the self-hosted category is Nous Research’s Hermes Agent, which utilizes Docker, Modal, or Daytona backends and relies on SQLite FTS5 and local Markdown files for memory management. OpenClaw, originally launched as Clawdbot by Peter Steinberger in November 2025, remains a top contender for its broad chat-channel integration and flexible hosting options, ranging from free MIT-licensed local deployments to managed services costing $12–$49 per month.

Managed agents from major tech incumbents prioritize integration with existing ecosystems. Google’s Gemini Spark ($19.99/mo) leverages Google Workspace context, while OpenAI’s 'dots' agent integrates with ChatGPT memory and Codex, offering proactive research capabilities with read-only constraints. Meta’s Muse agent utilizes a secure cloud VM architecture with a 'Sentinel' gatekeeper to manage internet access and user approvals for sensitive actions like email or purchases. Security across these platforms is evaluated based on isolation boundaries, default permission sets, and the presence of human-in-the-loop approval gates for high-stakes tasks.
takeaways: **Hermes Agent Architecture:** Utilizes SQLite FTS5 for session search and stores memory in local MEMORY.md and USER.md files, operating on user-managed infrastructure via Docker, Modal, or Daytona.

**OpenClaw Evolution:** Originally a weekend project named Clawdbot by Peter Steinberger in November 2025, it has transitioned to the OpenClaw Foundation with support for both self-hosted and managed deployments.
**Gemini Spark Pricing:** Positioned as a $19.99/month add-on for Google AI Pro users, specifically optimized for deep integration with Google Workspace data.
**Meta Muse Security:** Employs a 'Sentinel' agent gatekeeper to restrict internet access and enforce mandatory user approvals for external actions like email transmission or financial transactions.

**Evaluation Criteria:** Agents are ranked based on memory persistence/editability, security isolation boundaries, and total cost of ownership (subscription fees vs. token/hosting costs) as of November 21, 2026.

title: SAE-Audit: Clinical-Trial Prediction via Inference-Time Optimization of Black-Box LLMs Audited by Sparse Autoencoder Evidence
author: Junbo Shen
contentSnippet: Clinical trials are costly and often take years to complete, making early outcome prediction valuable for trial planning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to forecast clinical-trial outcomes, yet their predictions remain unreliable and their rationales may not faithfully reflect the evidence underlying their answers. On tasks such as predicting whether a registered clinical trial will complete or terminate early, frontier LLMs perform only modestly above chance in our experiments. We introduce SAE-Audit, which optimizes a black-box LLM at inference time with evidence obtained from a deployable open model. A frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is converted into a vocabulary of clinical concepts. Sparse probes fitted on past trials determine which concepts are associated with the outcome. For a new protocol, the concepts detected by the probe are written as evidence, each with the direction and strength of its association with the outcome, and the LLM being audited optimizes its answer in the light of this evidence. Without additional training, SAE-Audit raises balanced accuracy of deepseek-v4-flash by 9.6--12.0 points on five clinical-trial prediction tasks and raises GPT-5.6-terra by 8.0 points on trial completion, exceeding other agentic inference-time optimization methods by a large margin. As an auxiliary, SAE probes module within SAE-Audit is itself accurate and auditable, providing natural-language explanations directly derived from verified concept contributions and protocol evidence, without requiring additional LLMs at inference time. SAE-Audit provides verifiable, concept-level evidence for more accurate and auditable clinical-trial prediction. It can also be embedded into biomedical AI agents such as Biomni to optimize their performance.

title: Google AI Previews Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API for Large Tool Libraries
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Google has launched Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API , now in preview in the Interactions API. Gemini API Tool Retrieval lets an agent keep a large tool library available. It does not send every parameter schema in every prompt. The model loads a schema only when a task needs that tool. For agents wired to dozens of functions or MCP servers, it targets a real cost: tool definitions. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Tool: An API feature with no stated tool cap. Google advises static loading under 20 stable tools. Runs on: Google’s servers (server-side search) or your own registry (client-side). Interactions API, v1beta only. Performance: Search, schema load and function call resolve in 1 API request in server mode. Best: 0 extra round trips and no index to host for server-side retrieval. What is Gemini API Tool Retrieval? Tool Retrieval is a Gemini API feature that defers tool parameter schemas until the model asks for them. Google’s documentation states the problem plainly. A few dozen function declarations can consume tens of thousands of tokens on every request. With deferral, the model sees only each tool’s name and a short description. It does not see the parameter schema until retrieval. How does defer_loading work in the Gemini Interactions API? You add {"type": "tool_search"} to the tools array. Then you set defer_loading: true on each function to hold back. The @googledevs launch post shows a deferred issue_refund function on gemini-4-hydrogen . Its code comment mentions 50+ other deferred functions. When the model needs a deferred tool, the response contains 3 steps: tool_search_call : the model requests a tool by name. tool_search_result : the API returns the full schema. function_call : the model emits the call your code executes. The API resolves the first 2 steps itself. Your app only runs the function_call and returns a function_result . Deferred functions can carry an optional short_description . It is shown during retrieval and is valid only when defer_loading is true. Server-side vs client-side retrieval Server-side is the default. Gemini runs the search, so there is no index to build or host. Client-side mode uses "execution": "client" . Your app runs its own lookup, such as an embedding index, registry or permission filter. It returns matching declarations in functi

summary.tldr:
Google has introduced 'Tool Retrieval' for the Gemini API, currently in preview within the Interactions API (v1beta). This feature addresses the token overhead associated with large tool libraries by deferring the loading of parameter schemas until the model specifically requests them. By only providing the tool name and a short description in the initial prompt, developers can avoid consuming tens of thousands of tokens per request, which is a common bottleneck when managing dozens of functions or MCP servers.

Technically, the implementation involves setting 'defer_loading: true' on functions and adding '{"type": "tool_search"}' to the tools array. The process operates in three steps: the model emits a 'tool_search_call', the API returns the full schema via 'tool_search_result', and finally, the model emits the 'function_call'. In server-side mode, the API handles the search, schema load, and function call resolution within a single API request, eliminating extra round trips. For more complex requirements, a client-side mode allows developers to manage their own lookup logic, such as embedding indices or permission filters, by setting 'execution: "client"'.
takeaways: **Token Efficiency:** Prevents large tool libraries from consuming excessive tokens by hiding parameter schemas until the model explicitly requires them.
**Implementation:** Requires adding '{"type": "tool_search"}' to the tools array and setting 'defer_loading: true' on individual function declarations.
**Deployment Modes:** Supports server-side retrieval (default, no index hosting required) and client-side retrieval (custom lookup logic via 'execution: "client"').
**Usage Recommendation:** Google advises static loading for scenarios involving fewer than 20 stable tools, while Tool Retrieval is intended for larger, dynamic libraries.
**API Workflow:** The API automatically resolves the search and schema retrieval steps, leaving the developer to handle only the final 'function_call' and 'function_result'.

title: WAFT: A Fourier-Analytic Framework for Steady-State Performance of Walker Constellations
author: Haoyang Xue
contentSnippet: The Walker configuration is predominantly adopted by nongeostationary orbit constellations exemplified by Starlink and Kuiper. The steady-state distribution of aggregate downlink interference power is critical for spectrum coexistence regulation. Large-scale time-stepped simulation and stochastic geometry (SG)-based models are the mainstream methods for obtaining the distribution, but are either computationally expensive or subject to inherent bias. This paper models the aggregate downlink interference power as an additive observable and proposes the Walker-constellation Analysis via Fourier Transform (WAFT) framework to derive the steady-state performance. Modeling the constellation as a periodic impulse array on the phase torus, the spectral representation of the observable is derived via 2-D Fourier analysis. Analytical expressions for the expectation, variance, and steady-state complementary cumulative distribution function are further derived, and the periodicity of receiver performance along longitude is characterized. For a Starlink sub-constellation example, numerical validation shows that the percentile discrepancies of WAFT relative to a finite-duration time-stepped simulation remain within 0.09~dB. Comparisons with isotropic and intensity-matched SG models reveal that the conditional independence of satellite positions alone makes the models assign a substantial probability mass to physically infeasible values, producing percentile discrepancies.

title: Edit-Induced Dependency Mismatch: Propagation Omissions, Recovery, and Evaluation Blind Spots in Coding Agents
author: Fei Ding
contentSnippet: During iterative code modification, coding agents may continue to rely in subsequent reasoning on outdated dependency judgments whose text remains fixed in the context, leading to errors in subsequent reasoning and leaving consumer defects undetected by the original task evaluations, thereby exposing blind spots in the tested benchmarks. We study actual agent execution trajectories collected on benchmark tasks: deepseek-v4-flash runs on DeepSWE and SWE-bench Verified, supplemented by Qwen3.8-Flash cases on FeatureBench. Focusing on edit-induced consumer obligations, a full-corpus blinded human audit of the DeepSWE runs identifies terminal mismatches, including diagnoses whose task scope remains disputed. Following supplementary execution checks, all retained DeepSWE terminal events have execution support. The audit also shows that recovery within a trajectory can coexist with terminal omissions in the same run. The process analysis links the presentation of relevant consumer code to explicit dependency judgments and subsequent synchronization actions recorded in the trajectories. An explicit dependency-review prompt reduces terminal omissions under the tested conditions, supporting re-derivation of consumer obligations after edits. Local replays of selected DeepSWE cases show that synchronizing the diagnosed consumers restores the target behavior while the listed controls continue to pass. Cross-benchmark execution counterexamples show that the original task evaluations do not fully detect edit-induced dependency mismatches: patches pass those evaluations, yet additional execution checks confirm unintended defects along existing consumer paths. These findings support measuring task scores, terminal propagation states, and recovery separately.

summary.tldr:

We study actual agent execution trajectories collected on benchmark tasks: deepseek-v4-flash runs on DeepSWE and SWE-bench Verified, supplemented by Qwen3.8-Flash cases on FeatureBench. Focusing on edit-induced consumer obligations, a full-corpus blinded human audit of the DeepSWE runs identifies terminal mismatches, including diagnoses whose task scope remains disputed.

Following supplementary execution checks, all retained DeepSWE terminal events have execution support. The audit also shows that recovery within a trajectory can coexist with terminal omissions in the same run. The process analysis links the presentation of relevant consumer code to explicit dependency judgments and subsequent synchronization actions recorded in the trajectories.
